examples.summary: The class-file writer encodes every string constant into modified UTF-8 with `ModifiedUtf8#encodeInto`, which tests each `char` for the one-, two- or three-byte form. Most constants are ASCII, so a developer adds a fast path: a leading run of one-byte characters, recognised by `(char) (c - 1) < 0x7f`, is copied without the general test, and the general loop takes over at the first character that is not. The regression proof against the previous version, which JBMC could not finish at the default bound of eight characters in 2.8 GB, is done by the tool's own checker in 7 s and 76 MB: once the search has grown past a few hundred paths, the paths through the loops are merged at their join points, so the proof explores 733 paths where there are 11643, and at a bound of twelve characters it is done in 83 s where the unmerged search exhausted its budget of 200000 paths without a verdict.
notes: This proof waited from 1 to 4 November 2026 in `examples/apps/mica/pending` for a machine with more memory: JBMC at `--max-array-length 8 --unwind 16` ran out of memory at 2.8 GB in 15 s (and at 5.7 GB before a limit was set), and at bounds 2, 3 and 4 proved the versions equal in 31, 94 and 275 s. The tool's own checker proves it at the default bound in 7 s and 76 MB, and at twelve characters in 83 s and 155 MB, so the pending proof became this example and example 143.

Path merging in the tool's own checker is what this example exercises: without it the checker explores 11643 paths with 46063 solver calls in 5.6 s at the bound of eight, and at a bound of twelve exhausts its budget of 200000 paths after 128 s with no verdict. Merged after the first 512 paths, the search is 733 paths at eight and 868 at twelve; merged from the start it is 237 and 369. The time at eight does not fall, because the solver's work moves: the comparisons of the output cells at the end of the harness, one per element of each version's copy, are each a proof over the merged formula, and the sixteen of them take most of the 7 s. At sixteen the search merged from the start had 488 paths and 678 solver calls after four minutes and no verdict, each call over a formula of 163000 variables, where the unmerged search had spent its path budget after 145 s; the bound the proof scales to on this machine is twelve. The first 512 paths are left unmerged because a small search is cheaper that way: a solver call about one concrete path is cheap, one about a disjunction of paths is not, and the 64-bit arithmetic of examples 131, 134 and 139 took two to three times as long merged from the start.

The bound applies to `chars` and `out` alike, so an input whose encoding needs more bytes than `out` holds overflows the buffer in both versions and is compared up to that exception; eight three-byte characters need 24 bytes and are never encoded to the end. A difference that only shows past the eighth byte written would not be seen. Example 143's difference shows in the first byte.

The fast path's test `(char) (chars[i] - 1) < 0x7f` is one comparison for the two the general loop makes (`c >= 0x0001 && c <= 0x007f`): the subtraction wraps U+0000 to U+FFFF, which fails the test, as it should, since U+0000 takes the two-byte form. The proof covers the wrap, since `chars` has every value in its cells.

The encoder's properties in `properties.contract` (examples 044, 048 and 055) hold of both versions; they say how many bytes are written and what the first byte of each character is, not that the new version writes what the old one wrote. The regression proof is a different statement, which the properties do not imply either way: example 143 is a fast path the properties allow and the regression proof refutes.

Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 5 November 2026, JDK 25.0.4.1, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 1 method the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict.

examples.title: An ASCII fast path that admits U+0080 writes it in one byte, which the properties allow
examples.summary: The class-file writer's `ModifiedUtf8#encodeInto` gains an ASCII fast path: a leading run of one-byte characters is copied without the general test. The test is written `(char) (c - 1) <= 0x7f`, which admits U+0080 along with U+0001 to U+007F, and writes it as the single byte `0x80`, where modified UTF-8 needs two: a class file with such a constant is rejected by the virtual machine. The encoder's committed properties, about how many bytes each character takes and what its first byte is, hold of the leading run too, since they are checked on the general loop's inputs; only the comparison with the previous version catches it. The tool's own checker refutes the proof in 1.1 s and 60 MB on `encodeInto(chars=['\u0080'], out=[32])`, with the paths past the first few hundred merged at their join points, where JBMC ran out of memory at the default bound.
notes: This is the planned example 058 of `examples/apps/mica/pending`, held from 1 to 4 November 2026 for a machine with more memory: JBMC refuted it at `--max-array-length 2 --unwind 6` in 6 s and at 4 and 8 in 38 s and 1.5 GB, and ran out of memory at 2.8 GB at the default bound of eight. The tool's own checker refutes it at the default bound in 1.1 s and 60 MB, and proves the corrected fast path (example 142) at the same bound.

The committed properties of `encodeInto` (examples 044, 048 and 055: the count of bytes written, the first byte of each character, the buffer not overrun) do not catch this. They are stated per character of the general loop's rule, and the fast path writes U+0080 as one byte where the properties' `encodedLength(c)` says two, so a property proof would catch it only if the property is written against the previous version's rule rather than the code's helpers; the regression proof needs no property at all. The pending README of 1 November predicted this: only comparing with the previous version catches it.

The witness is the smallest the interpreter's shrinking reaches: a one-character string and a one-byte buffer, on which the previous version throws for want of a second byte and the new one returns. The disagreement is in the first byte written, `0xC2` against `0x80`, so a longer buffer shows the same difference as different results, 2 against 1.

The search is 731 paths with 2055 solver calls (1.1 s): the first 512 on their own, the rest merged where they meet. Unmerged throughout, it found the same witness in 2364 paths with 8907 calls in 1.0 s; merged from the start, in 260 paths with 342 calls in 4.6 s, since each branch of a merged path is a question over every path merged into it and a violation is found only after every path that could reach the join has been merged, where a search going deep first can hit it early. That is why the checker merges only once a search has grown past a few hundred paths, where the paths would otherwise multiply (example 142's note).

Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 5 November 2026, JDK 25.0.4.1, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 1 method the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict.

examples.title: A short-table scan declared as the intended change, whose proof covers no table at the default bound
examples.summary: The interpreter's `lookupswitch` search gains a linear scan for tables of at most eight pairs, and the regression proof is asked to show the bisection unchanged on the rest: `--unchanged-unless 'matches.length <= 8'`. The default bound on array parameters is eight, so every table in the domain is among the intended inputs, the harness returns before calling either version, and the proof covers no input. The verdict is verified, vacuously, and the tool says so on a line of its own, found by running the statement with the calls replaced by the assertion's failure.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified, vacuously: no input in the domain reaches the calls
notes: The vacuity check is the tool's, whichever engine proved the statement: the probe is run by the tool's own checker over the statement's own domain, and the line appears under a JBMC proof as it does here. It is run only when the harness skips inputs before the calls, that is with `--unchanged-unless`, a record parameter or receiver whose constructor may reject an input, or `--before-arguments` that may throw; a harness that calls the versions on every input has nothing to probe. A `prove` with `--assume` is probed the same way. The probe took 0.0 s here, one path and no solver call, since `matches.length <= 8` is a constant under the bound. Here `python3 examples/tools/build.py` compares the expected verdict with the vacuity too: an example that is verified vacuously must say so in `expected.vacuous`, as the TLC examples of [tag tla-coverage](../README.md#tag-tla-coverage) do.

Why the bound defeats the scope: the scope is over the symbolic array's length, and the domain of a regression proof over arrays is every length up to `--max-array-length`, eight by default, the same number as the scan limit. The proof line prints both, `where !(matches.length <= 8)` and `matches: int[] of length ≤ 8`, and a reader who holds them side by side sees the proof is empty; the tool now holds them side by side for the reader. A scope over the elements can be emptied the same way, by a quantifier that no array up to the bound satisfies, and a scope over scalars by an expression that is a tautology, `skewSeconds >= 0 || skewSeconds < 0`, which is what the check first caught, on example 125's method.

The scan is correct, and the proof that shows it is the one with the sortedness scope, `--unchanged-unless '!(\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < matches.length - 1; matches[i] < matches[i + 1])'`: at bound eight the tool's own checker proves the new `find` equal to the old on every strictly sorted table of up to eight pairs and every key in 1.1 s, 88 paths, 660 solver calls, 46 MB, where the scan runs for every table and the bisection in the previous version; at bound twelve in 3.1 s, 180 paths, 67 MB. Without a scope the checker finds `find(matches=[20, 16], key=16)` in 0.08 s, -1 before (the bisection tests `matches[0] = 20 > 16` and moves `high` below the start) and 1 after (the scan reaches the second pair): on an unsorted table the two searches differ, as example 141 found for the half-open rewrite, and the scope states what every `lookupswitch` table satisfies.

The change is the shape of the JDK's own `DualPivotQuicksort`, which sorts small arrays by insertion sort below a constant threshold, and of many searches that scan short tables rather than bisect them: it is a performance change meant to preserve behaviour, and `behaviourChangeIntended` is false. Declaring the short tables as intended inputs is the mistake this example is about: it is the natural declaration for a reviewer who wants the bisection checked and takes the scan on trust, and it leaves the proof nothing when the bound is the threshold. The domain line of every proof names the bound for this reason.

Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 5 November 2026, JDK 25.0.4.1, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 2 methods the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict.

examples.title: The bound raised past the scan limit: the bisection proved unchanged on the tables the scope admits
examples.summary: Example 144's declaration with the bound on array parameters raised to twelve: the domain now holds tables of nine to twelve pairs, which the scope `matches.length <= 8` admits to the proof, and the tool's own checker proves the bisection unchanged on every such table and every key in 4 s. The vacuity line is gone, since the probe finds a table that reaches the calls. The proof is of the branch the change did not touch, which is what the declaration asked; the notes carry the proof of the scan itself.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change
notes: The two proofs together are the review of the change: this one, that the bisection is as it was on the tables the scan does not take; and the sortedness-scoped one of example 144's notes, that the scan agrees with the bisection on every strictly sorted table of up to eight pairs (1.1 s) or twelve (3.1 s). The second is the one a reviewer should ask for first; the first is what the declaration `matches.length <= 8` asks, and at the default bound it asks nothing (example 144).

Raising the bound is the right fix for a scope over the array's length, and a scope over scalars that is a tautology has no fix but rewriting it. Each length costs paths: 89 at twelve with the scope skipping eight of them, against 88 for the sortedness scope at eight and 180 at twelve. JBMC was not run on this example: it took 101 s and 2 GB for the sortedness scope at bound eight on example 141, and the own checker is the engine named.

The `maxArrayLength` field of `approach` is new with this example: it is the tool's `--max-array-length`, as `unwind` is its `--unwind`, for an example whose statement needs a bound other than the default eight. The bounds of twelve in example 142 and 143's notes were measured by hand; this field makes a bound part of the page the pipeline runs.

Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 5 November 2026, JDK 25.0.4.1, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 2 methods the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict.

examples.title: A timeout rule folded as dead code in a refactor is checked as built
examples.summary: The change of example 060, made as a refactor: a developer folds the leader's case of the election timeout into the follower's and candidate's, calls the leader's case dead code, and does not regenerate the role machine's contract, since nothing is meant to change. The tests pass. The election model is generated from the role machine's contract, and a runner that generated it from the committed contract unless a behaviour change was intended would check the old rule, and pass whatever the patch did. The runner derives the contract from the patched classes on every run instead: one case differs from the committed contract, which nobody approved, and the model, checked on the rule that was built, shows the leader deposing itself in four steps.
notes: The patch is example 060's. 060 declares the change as intended, so its contract is regenerated and approved; here it is declared as a refactor, which is the case the outside review of build.py (llm-dlc/loops/build-orchestration-review.md, section 1B) found unchecked: the model was generated from the committed contract unless `behaviourChangeIntended` was true.

Since 2026-11-05 every D1 run derives the contract of each generated operator from the patched classes and records the connection in `modelContracts`. A difference the change does not intend is a violation of its own, with the diff in `contractDiff` and a `contract-changed` result in the SARIF report, and TLC's own verdict is kept in `modelVerdict`.

Under the earlier runner this example's model would have been generated from the committed contract, so TLC would have checked the code before the patch. It was added with the runner change, and its first result comes from the verification pipeline.

examples.title: A contract that says Random.nextInt never throws is refuted on the JVM before the proof relies on it
examples.summary: Crosscut's retry filter gains full jitter: a wait drawn by `Random.nextInt` below a ceiling the base doubled by a shift kept short of the sign bit with `Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros`. The tool's own checker implements none of the three JDK calls, so under `--gaps advised` the agent driving it writes a contract for each. Its contract for `nextInt` says the call returns a value in [0, bound) and nothing else, which is true wherever this kernel calls it. The tool tests every contract on a real JVM before it relies on one: the JDK's `nextInt` throws `IllegalArgumentException` at `bound=0`, the contract is refused with the JVM's counterexamples, its gap stays open, and the proof stops there, with the other two contracts accepted.
notes: The proof reaches three calls the tool's own checker does not implement, each a gap with an id that names the JDK it is about: `jdk-static-method:java.lang.Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(I)I@jdk-25.0.4.1`, `jdk-constructor:java.util.Random.<init>(J)V@jdk-25.0.4.1` and `jdk-primitive-method:java.util.Random.nextInt(I)I@jdk-25.0.4.1`. Under `--gaps strict` or `assume` the run would end with no verdict: the two methods return a value the proof reads, which has no assume form. Under `--gaps advised` with no contracts the tool stops before solving with the three gaps, what a contract for each must state, and a template, which is where an agent starts (step 3a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`).

The contracts in `gaps.contracts` were written by an agent, the session that made this example (Claude Opus 5.5), from the template and the JDK's documentation of each call, and are marked so in their `written-by:` lines. Nothing in the library or the runner calls a model: the agent is whoever drives the tool, and the file is committed like any other.

The JVM test is the one that refutes it. The proof against the JDK's bytecode applies only to a static JDK method of primitive parameters, so it covers `numberOfLeadingZeros` and not the two `Random` calls, whose receiver's state it cannot see; those are tested and, at best, `tested`. The test calls `nextInt` on `new java.util.Random()`, the receiver its class's constructor of no arguments builds, since the JDK's `nextInt` throws on its argument alone.

Each of the 84 refuting inputs is a bound of zero or below; the advice keeps the first, `bound=0`, and four more as examples (`-1`, `-2`, `-2147483648`, `-2147483647`). The other 82 inputs return a value in [0, bound), as the contract says.

A contract the JVM refutes is refused even where it would give the right verdict, as here, because the tool cannot know where else it will be applied: example 148's proof, on the corrected contract, is the one that is about this kernel.

Checked inline when the example was written, on the patched module (the library's own run, not the recorded one): the three contracts were checked in about 0.2 s, and no solver ran. The recorded result is the pipeline's.

Nothing in the library or the runner calls a model: the agent is whoever drives the tool, and the file is committed like any other.

Example 147 is the same change with the agent's first contract for `nextInt`, which leaves out the exception: the JVM refutes it at `bound=0`, and the run stops with the gap open. This example is the run after the agent corrected it, the loop the advised mode is for: run, read the gaps, write contracts, run again.

Only the contract for `numberOfLeadingZeros` can be proved: a static JDK method whose parameters and result are primitives, in the checker's fragment, its class copied from the JDK image onto the proof's class path so that the checker runs its bytecode (18 paths, loops unwound 16 times). The `Random` calls have a receiver whose state the proof cannot see, so their contracts are tested, and the verdict counts them apart.

The contract for `numberOfLeadingZeros` has to say where the highest one bit is. A weaker one, `0 <= result && result <= 32`, is proved against the JDK's bytecode just as well, but the property does not follow from it: the checker then finds `fullJitterMillis(baseMillis=16, capMillis=20, attempt=14, requestId=20)`, on a result the weak contract admits and the JDK never returns for that base. A witness through a contract is one the contracts admit, and only the JVM's run says whether the JDK's calls give it.

The off-by-one, `Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(baseMillis)` without the `- 1`, is a violation on these contracts. The checker's witness `fullJitterMillis(baseMillis=99492, capMillis=100000, attempt=100000, requestId=100000)` shifts a 17-bit base by 15, to a negative ceiling, and `nextInt` throws `IllegalArgumentException("bound must be positive")`. examples.title: Full jitter proved on the contract library's contracts alone, checked once and not again by the run
examples.summary: The jitter of examples 147 and 148, proved with no contract of the agent's at all. The proof by the tool's own checker reaches two JDK calls it does not implement, `new Random(long)` and `Random.nextInt(int)`, and the tool's contract library closes each: its contracts for them were tested once on a real JVM, and the run applies them on the record of that check without checking them again. Under `--max-trust 0`, the policy CI uses, the proof may rest on no unchecked contract, and it rests on none.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input, relying on 2 contracts for gaps (2 tested)
notes: Example 148 is the same change with the agent's own contracts in `gaps.contracts`, which the run checks itself (as written, a proof of one against the JDK's bytecode and a JVM test of all three, about 0.2 s; what it shows now that `numberOfLeadingZeros` is no gap waits on its rerun, VF-002). examples.title: A retry throttle rewritten with min and max proved equal on every throttle its constructor makes
examples.summary: Crosscut's retry throttle (gRPC's retry throttling: a failure takes a token, a success gives back the token ratio, retries only while more than half the tokens are left) is a mutable object every call on a channel shares. `recorded` is rewritten in the form gRPC's Java client uses, one clamp with `Math.max` and `Math.min` and the threshold doubled instead of halved. The regression proof takes the throttle as an object made by its constructor from symbolic limits, compares the result and the throttle's fields as both versions leave them, and proves them equal on every input, the claim saying that its throttles are the ones the constructor makes: full ones.
notes: The domain is objects made by their constructor (decision 2 of llm-dlc/loops/foundations.md): `Throttle(ThrottleLimits)` starts full, `maxTokens * 1000` thousandths, so the proof is over one outcome on a full throttle, for every limit the record accepts (1 to 1000 tokens, a ratio of 1 to 1000000 thousandths). A throttle drained by earlier failures is a state no constructor makes; the claim covers none, and its headline and domain say so instead of 'every input'. 152 is the rewrite that differs only there, and is verified by the same proof for the same reason.

Observed: the boolean result, the exception, the throttle's fields as the call leaves them, and the identity relations among the throttle, its limits and the result (`stated.observations.objects` lists `throttle: limits.maxTokens, limits.tokenRatioMilli, milliTokens`). The `ThrottleLimits` record is a value, compared by its components only.

`Math.max` and `Math.min` are taken by the tool's own checker as the JDK computes them, so the proof needs no contract and no JBMC; JBMC cannot take an object input at all (`approach.engine`: native).
Pairs with 151 (the same kernel's `reconfigured`, its alias turned into a copy, refuted) and 152 (this rewrite without the floor at zero, outside the claim).

examples.title: A throttle kept across a config update turned into a copy loses the failures of the calls in flight
examples.summary: When a channel's service config is updated with the same retry limits, `reconfigured` hands back the channel's throttle itself, so the calls in flight, which hold it, keep counting their failures into the throttle the channel goes on using. The change hands back a copy with the same tokens and the same limits instead: every field agrees when it returns, and a failure recorded afterwards by a call in flight goes into the old object, which nothing reads, so a failing backend gets retries the throttle would have refused. The regression proof observes the identity relations within each version and refutes the change with `result == throttle`, which holds before and not after; the witness is a construction recipe, replayed in the interpreter and run on a JVM.
notes: This is the alias-to-copy defect of llm-dlc/loops/foundations.md: an alias turned into a copy with identical primitive values, which a caller sees only by mutating one. Physical object ids are never compared across versions; the identity relation is compared within each version, and the witness's two replays read alike but for it.

The copy reuses the same `ThrottleLimits` object, so `result.limits == throttle.limits` holds in both versions and is no part of the difference; a copy made with `new ThrottleLimits(...)` would differ there too, but a record of primitive components is a value and is compared by components only.

The witness is run on a JVM after the interpreter's replay (`replayed in the interpreter and run on a JVM (JDK …), where the harness fails on it too`): the harness makes each version's throttle from the same leaves, and reads the classes' package-private fields through opened copies of them, which the JVM run loads first on its class path.
Pairs with 150 (the same kernel's `recorded`, rewritten correctly and proved) and 152 (a rewrite of `recorded` that differs only outside the constructor-made domain).

examples.title: A throttle that drops its floor at zero is proved only on full throttles, where it cannot differ
examples.summary: The same rewrite of `recorded` as 150, but the floor at zero tokens is gone: `Math.min(next, ceiling)` without the `Math.max(0, …)`. A failure on a drained throttle now takes it below zero, and every token below zero is ten more successes (at a ratio of 0.1) before the channel may retry again: after three failures on a two-token throttle it takes 21 successes instead of 11. The regression proof verifies the change, because its throttles are made by their constructor, which makes them full, and one failure never drains a full throttle; the verdict says `on every input of constructor-made objects` and the domain names the constructor, so the result is a claim about full throttles only, not a proof that the rewrite is right.
notes: This is the planted defect 'a bug only in a state outside the constructor-made domain, which must show as outside the claim, not as proved' of llm-dlc/loops/foundations.md. The question it answers: can the way inputs are made hide the bug? It can, and so the result names the domain in its headline (`every input of constructor-made objects`, not `every input`), in its domain line, and in its constructible assumption; a reader who takes the verdict as 'the rewrite is right' has dropped those words.

Shown on a JVM by hand, not by the run: `new Throttle(new ThrottleLimits(2, 100))`, three failures, then successes until `recorded` returns true. The unpatched build leaves 1000, 0, 0 thousandths and allows a retry after 11 successes; the patched one 1000, 0, -1000 and 21.
Pairs with 150 (the same rewrite with the floor, proved by the same proof) and 151 (an alias turned into a copy, refuted by an identity relation).

examples.title: A refill helper rewritten as whole periods, proved once and one function in its caller's proof
examples.summary: Crosscut's `TokenBucket.lastAfter`, the time up to which a refill has credited the bucket, is rewritten from `now - (now - last) % period` to `last + (now - last) / period * period`, the whole periods counted and added back. Its caller, the `Retry-After` of a refused request, is unchanged. Run with the proof cache, the regression proof of the caller first proves the helper's two versions equal on every input, as a check of its own, and stores that proof. It then takes the helper as one function in both versions of the caller, whose statement names the helper's proof by its claim key. Where example 120 shares a helper because its bytecode is identical, this one shares a helper that changed, on the strength of its own proof.
notes: Why the proof can take the helper's new version for both: the helper's own proof is over every input of its parameter types, so every call, in either version and with any arguments, is in its domain, and the two versions have the same outcome there, a result or the same exception. Neither reads or writes state. The previous version with its calls redirected therefore behaves exactly as written, and the caller's proof is exact: a counterexample under the redirection would be a real one, and no refinement is needed. A helper proof over a narrower domain (`--unchanged-unless`, mapped arguments, a relation between results) is never used, since it would need an assertion at each call.

Measured when the example was written, on the development machine: the helper's proof took 0.19 s (2 paths, 2 solver calls), and the caller's with the helper as one function 0.00 s (3 paths, 2 solver calls). Without the cache, the caller's proof runs through both versions of the helper as written and takes 1.2 s (4 solver calls) for the same verdict. A second run with the same cache is an exact hit of the caller's claim, and a second caller of the helper would find the helper's proof in the cache. The recorded run starts from an empty cache, so its proof line says the helper was proved now.

The helper's proof is a regression proof like any other, and its key is the one a check of `TokenBucket#lastAfter` alone gets: the library's tests check both, and that a caller's key does not depend on when or where the helper's proof was made.

Without `--cache` the tool proves nothing of a changed helper, and runs the caller through both versions of it, which is what every recorded example did before this one. The cache is the proof's only source of helper evidence, and it is local: a directory under the build, filled by this run and never committed.
Example 161 is the sibling with the helper's change wrong: its own proof is refuted, the helper stays as written, and the caller's proof finds the regression.

Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 7 November 2026, JDK 25.0.5, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 3 methods the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict.

The job is resubmitted as `20261107-163050-example-160-a-changed-refill-helper-prov`.

examples.title: A refill helper aligned to the clock's grid, refuted alone, and its caller sends a client back early
examples.summary: Crosscut's `TokenBucket.lastAfter` is rewritten to credit the bucket up to the start of the period the clock reading falls in, `now - now % period`, as the fixed window aligns its start. A bucket's periods are counted from its last refill, not from the clock's zero, so the credited time moves whenever the last refill is off the clock's grid. Run with the proof cache, the proof first checks the helper on its own and refutes it, so the helper stays as written in both versions. The caller's proof, the `Retry-After` of a refused request, then finds a client told to wait 1 ns where the old code said 2, which comes back and is refused again. The tests pass, and so does the caller's property that the wait is never more than a period.
notes: The tests miss it because every refill in `TokenBucketTest` and `RetryAfterTest` starts at `lastNanos = 0`, which is on every grid, where the two forms agree. The property of `nanosUntilToken` in `properties.contract`, a wait of nothing or more than nothing and at most a period, holds of the new version too, since the wait to the end of the grid's period is within a period as well. The property of `lastAfter`, that the credited time never falls behind the last refill, does not hold of the new version (credited 0 after a refill at 1, by the arithmetic), so a property proof of the helper would find it. The regression proof of the caller finds it with no property written.

The helper's own counterexample lies outside the module's precondition, with the clock reading before the last refill, since the helper's proof covers every input and the shrinker keeps the smallest. That is enough to keep the helper out of the narrow class: a proof restricted to its callers' domain would need the caller's proof to assert, at each call, that the arguments are in that domain, which this form of sharing does not do.

With the helper refuted, the caller's proof is the one it would be without the cache: both versions of the helper as written, the regression found in a few tenths of a second when the example was written.

Example 160 is the sibling whose helper change is right: its own proof holds, and the caller is proved with the helper as one function in both versions. Example 132 is a regression on the other refill helper, `tokensAfter`, counting periods from the clock's zero.

Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 7 November 2026, JDK 25.0.5, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 3 methods the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict.

The job is resubmitted as `20261107-163051-example-161-a-refill-helper-aligned-to-t`.

examples.title: A retry route and its policy refactored, proved to send what they sent, in order, on every input
examples.summary: A webhook dispatcher's failure route and the Crosscut retry policy behind it are both rewritten: the policy as one expression over two helpers, the route around the policy's answer with each Kafka send in a method of its own. The tool proves, for every status, idempotency and attempt count, that the route answers the same status and attempts the same sends, to the same topics with the same payloads in the same order, as before.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: the trace of boundary calls, the response and the outcome preserved on every input
notes: Checked by `jvmcontract effects`, which build.py runs as the B9 check of the route app (`run_tool_effects`): every entry point of the unpatched build against its counterpart in the patched one, under the claim its own observation spec makes. Run inline on 2026-11-07 (JDK 25.0.5): `POST /deliveries/failures` verified, with the result, exception, status and `KafkaTemplate.send` observations preserved, proved by the tool's own checker in 0.1 s (0.4 s for the whole command) over `status: int × idempotent: boolean × attempts: int`.

The route sends two classes of payload through one `KafkaTemplate.send`, a `RetryScheduled` and a `DeadLettered`, so the recording stub reads each payload path through the class the payload is (`data.attempt` is absent from a dead letter, `data.attempts` from a retry) and snapshots the class itself as `data.class`, so that a retry and a dead letter with equal values are different attempts. Before this example the narrow case refused such a call ("the call sites pass 2 classes of argument, and a stub reads one").

The kernel's rewrite is proved through the route, not on its own: `status / 100 == 5` is the same test as `status >= 500 && status <= 599` on every `int`, negative ones included, since Java's division truncates toward zero (-599 / 100 is -5), and the proof covers every status, not only the HTTP range.

What the proof assumes, as the verifier output lists it: `KafkaTemplate.send` is a recording stub in both builds that returns normally (an attempt is a call made, not a delivery), `DeliveryFailures` is made by its constructor with a null template, and at most four attempts are recorded, exactly in order.
The siblings 171 and 172 are this refactor with one defect each: a dropped dead letter, and a duplicated one.

examples.title: A retry route that skips the dead letter for a client error loses the delivery without a trace
examples.summary: The same refactor of the failure route and its retry policy, with one shortcut added: a 4xx other than 408 and 429 answers 200 at once, since no retry fixes it. The answer is the same as before and every test passes, but the delivery is no longer dead-lettered. The effect check finds a request on which the old route sends a dead letter and the new one sends nothing, and replays it on a JVM.
notes: Checked by `jvmcontract effects`, which build.py runs as the B9 check of the route app (`run_tool_effects`). Run inline on 2026-11-07 (JDK 25.0.5): refuted. The checker found `status=416, idempotent=true, attempts=0` in its second search stage ([-100000:100000]: no status in [0, 20] is a client error) and shrank it in 27 interpreter runs to `status=400, idempotent=false, attempts=0`, on which both builds answer 200, the old one attempting `KafkaTemplate.send(topic="delivery-dead-letters", data.status=400, data.attempts=0, ...)` and the new one no modeled call; replayed on the JVM under the recording stubs.

The observations other than the send are unresolved, not preserved, in the result: a refutation of the log shows that the logs differ, not which of the other observations still agree. The answer does agree here (200 in both), which is the point of the example: a proof of the answer alone would pass.

`attempts=0` is outside what a dispatcher reports (one attempt at least), and the proof's domain is every `int` the parameter binds; the defect shows on every client error other than 408 and 429, whatever the attempt count.
The tests pass: they look at the answer and at the last record sent, and none reports a client error.

The route sends two classes of payload through one `KafkaTemplate.send`, a `RetryScheduled` and a `DeadLettered`, so the recording stub reads each payload path through the class the payload is (`data.attempt` is absent from a dead letter, `data.attempts` from a retry) and snapshots the class itself as `data.class`, so that a retry and a dead letter with equal values are different attempts. Before this example the narrow case refused such a call ("the call sites pass 2 classes of argument, and a stub reads one").

examples.title: A retry route that dead-letters a delivery out of attempts sends the dead letter twice
examples.summary: The same refactor of the failure route and its retry policy, with the case of a delivery out of attempts handled first: it is dead-lettered whatever the receiver answered, and the route then goes on to ask the policy, which refuses, and dead-letters it again. The answer is the same and every test passes; the effect check finds the duplicate send, in exact order, and replays it on a JVM.
notes: Checked by `jvmcontract effects`, which build.py runs as the B9 check of the route app (`run_tool_effects`). Run inline on 2026-11-07 (JDK 25.0.5): refuted. The checker found `status=20, idempotent=true, attempts=20` in its first search stage ([0:20]) and shrank it in 19 interpreter runs to `status=0, idempotent=false, attempts=5`, on which both builds answer 200, the old one attempting one `send` to `delivery-dead-letters` and the new one the same send twice; replayed on the JVM under the recording stubs.
The trace is compared in exact order and in number, so two equal attempts are not one: the check would not pass a duplicate even if the payloads were all that a consumer looked at.
The tests pass: `deadLettersADeliveryOutOfAttempts` looks at the last record sent, which is the right dead letter. A test that counted the records sent would catch it.

The route sends two classes of payload through one `KafkaTemplate.send`, a `RetryScheduled` and a `DeadLettered`, so the recording stub reads each payload path through the class the payload is (`data.attempt` is absent from a dead letter, `data.attempts` from a retry) and snapshots the class itself as `data.class`, so that a retry and a dead letter with equal values are different attempts. Before this example the narrow case refused such a call ("the call sites pass 2 classes of argument, and a stub reads one").

examples.title: A quote's amount made a value object, proved at its route and in its kernel with no mapping written
examples.summary: A pricing kernel's quote changes its amount from a long of cents to a `Money` value object, and its discount helper is rewritten. The tool compares the two builds whole: the route `POST /quotes` answers the same total and sends the same event on every request, and the kernel's `total` and `withQuantity` do what they did under a relation between the old and new quotes that it inferred itself; the rewritten helper is proved once and used as one function in `total`'s proof, and a rerun is an exact hit of every proof.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: preserved on every input of the stated domain, with nothing written by hand
notes: Checked by `jvmcontract compare`, which build.py runs as the B9 check of the shop app (`run_tool_compare`): the unpatched build against the patched one, twice under one fresh proof cache, the verdict read from the rerun and the page's output from the first run. The verdict is the subject's; the page lists every other part the run checked.

The joint example of `llm-dlc/loops/foundations.md`'s Phase 5, made an example: the app's sources are the fixture's `before` build (`lib/tests/fixtures/foundations/`), and the patch turns them into its `after` build. `lib/tests/compare.rs` holds `jvmcontract compare` to the same builds inline; this is the same run by build.py, with the app's tests run too.

Nothing in the run is written by hand. The entry points' external inputs (`cents`, `quantity`) are anchored by their observation specs, so no mapping is involved at the boundary. The kernel's relation between the old and new quotes (`old.q.cents == new.q.amount.cents`, `old.q.quantity == new.q.quantity`) is alignment's proposal, inferred from how the two constructors route their parameters into the fields; it stays *proposed*, its evidence the proof under its claim key, and since nothing external anchors a kernel method's inputs, a proved relation there is reported as proved and not as the intended one.

What stays unresolved in every example of the set, by name: `POST /quotes/text` (its string concatenation isn't modeled), `Quote#cents` moved to `Money#cents` (a method of a class the old build doesn't have) and `Quote#quantity`, whose receiver is made differently in the two versions (`Quote(long, int)` before, `Quote(Money, int)` now), which the regression check doesn't relate yet. Before the application-core merge (2026-11-08) it was refused as an instance method instead; the merge's check takes a receiver made by its constructor, of the same construction in both versions.

Run inline on 2026-11-07 (JDK 25.0.5), `jvmcontract compare` on the app compiled unpatched and patched, as build.py compiles it, and on the fixture's builds, with the same verdicts (the times are the fixture's): `POST /quotes` verified, its result, exception, status and event preserved; `Pricing#total`, `Pricing#withQuantity` and `Pricing#discount` verified, `total`'s proof using `discount`'s; 8 obligations, 7 preserved and 1 unresolved (`POST /quotes/text`); no decision made by a person and no question asked. 0.5 s cold; the rerun took 0.2 s, every proof an exact hit under the first run's claim key.

The stale-cache defect is not an example of its own, since it needs two runs on different claims: `lib/tests/effects.rs` (`an_effect_proof_is_reused_exactly_when_its_claim_is_unchanged`) and `lib/tests/compare.rs` show the route's proof missed under a changed trace bound, snapshot, `@ResponseStatus` or handler, and each kernel defect proved again rather than reused.

The siblings 191 to 196 are this refactor with one defect each, every one aimed at an automation layer that could make it disappear: an offset an inferred mapping could absorb (191), an alias turned into a copy (192), a dropped event (193), a duplicated one (194), a bug only outside the constructor-made domain (195), and a renamed route (196).

examples.title: CVE-2023-34055: Unbounded HTTP method labels in web metrics
examples.summary: Spring Boot 2.7.17 → 2.7.18, fixed by 5490e739: WebMvcTags.method emitted the raw HTTP method token as a metric label. A deep negative packet: the release pair selected and source-locked, a frozen bounded-label property shared by the vulnerable and fixed tasks, preservation of the eight known names and the null request, an independent oracle, a request carrier and driver, and a mutation control. All four proof tasks are decided by jvmcontract's own checker on the released JARs, each as expected: the property is refuted on 2.7.17 and on the mutant, established on 2.7.18, and the known labels are proved preserved between the two releases.
examples.verdictLabel: ✗ unbounded on 2.7.17 and on the mutant (label ""); ✓ bounded on 2.7.18; ✓ known labels preserved
notes: The packet (N1 of llm-dlc/loops/example-targets-negative.md, 2026-11-14): target.json's tasks replay, vulnerable-security (expected refuted), fixed-security (expected established, the same claim file) and preservation (expected established outside the allowed change), all native strict and requiring the replay; sources.lock.json; claims/; replay/ (carrier, adapter, driver); controls/ (oracle, probes, mutation patch). README.md says how they fit.

The release pair is the execution pair, chosen before the claims were frozen: the exact-fix pair has no published artifact, while v2.7.17's WebMvcTags.java is the fix parent's blob (e5e2147b) and v2.7.18's the fix's (9f92c1ce), the sources JARs carry the same blobs, and Tag, ImmutableTag and HttpMethod are byte-identical across the two releases' closures, so within the method's reach the two releases differ by the fix alone.

The frozen label set is version-specific: spring-web 5.3's HttpMethod has GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE (one source blob in 5.3.30 and 5.3.31), so the fix labels CONNECT, a standard method, UNKNOWN, and resolves case-sensitively (get is UNKNOWN). Both are recorded as the release's behaviour, not judged.

The claim fixes the set and the eight names' own labels, not the label of a token inside the allowed change: a case-folding fix (get to GET) would satisfy both claims too. That is what the patch's intent supports; a stronger per-token claim would be another claim.

Developer note, not evidence (2026-11-14, before runtime's acquisition is merged): the JARs of sources.lock.json fetched by hand from Maven Central (sha1 checked against Central, sha256 as recorded), the carrier, adapter and driver compiled with --release 21, the mutant built from controls/raw-method-fallback.patch, and each revision run in its own JVM on Temurin 21.0.13 and 25.0.5 over the 15 probes. controls/oracle.py check: 2.7.17 fails the property at exactly the five triggers (xscf, lowercase-get, empty-token, long-token, connect) with every legitimate probe passing; 2.7.18 holds and passes; the mutant fails at the same five and passes the legitimate probes, reading getMethod() twice; oracle.py compare 2.7.17 → 2.7.18 is preserved, with the changes only inside the allowed region; each revision's per-probe lines were identical on 21 and 25. No exception, and no probe reached the request beyond getMethod().

Not in the claim: a request whose getMethod() returns null (no container produces one; 2.7.17 would throw NullPointerException from ImmutableTag, 2.7.18 return UNKNOWN), WebFluxTags.method (the same commit, but there the fix trusts ServerHttpRequest.getMethod(), so its property rests on the server adapter's classification, another obligation), the uri, status, outcome and exception tags, total metric cardinality and the application's availability.

Imported on 2026-11-14 from the archived registry (llm-dlc/loops/example-targets-inputs/spring-cve-targets.research-2026-11-04.json, as of 2026-11-04, rank 1, priority P0): nothing was built, replayed or proved. Its capability notes are from verifier 4c279ba6 and are stale; the blockers in target.json are predictions.
Benign behaviour to preserve (research): Each supported HTTP method retains its correct label; preserve the documented null-request behavior of the MVC variant.

Proof boundary (research): Bounds only the method-label dimension. Total metric cardinality and application availability require additional properties. A preclassified enum-only adapter does not verify classification of raw HTTP strings.

Feasibility (research): Best first capability spike. Small control flow, but original bytecode still needs String, enum, interface-call, Tag object and class-initialization support. Both classes have unrelated static initialization that must remain soundly modeled.
Registry note: Boot 3.x mitigation also updates Spring Framework for the related observation vulnerability. This benchmark deliberately chooses the Boot 2.7 implementation.

Revisions checked against upstream on 2026-11-14: the release tags resolved to commits, the fix commit and its parent read from github.com, the fix an ancestor of v2.7.18 and not of v2.7.17; on the same day WebMvcTags.java's blobs read at all four revisions (sources.lock.json).

Mutation control as a revision (2026-11-14, example-targets Phase 5): controls/raw-method-fallback.patch is declared in target.json as workflow W1's constructed revision `mutant` (base `fixed-release`, the patch's sha256 locked), the after of the `mutation` pair. It has two tasks of its own: `mutant-replay`, the concrete controls on that pair, where the base must hold and the mutant fail the oracle, and `mutant-security`, fixed-security's claim on the mutant, expected refuted. Its claim is bound to the mutant's artifact (runtime's identity `mutant:<base commit>+<patch sha256>`), never to a release's. It used to be only a `controls` entry on `fixed-release`, which no task prepared.

Runner interface (2026-11-14, example-targets Phase 5 step 1, request 9): controls/oracle.py also defines driver_args(), the driver's whole argument vector (the same as `oracle.py argv`), and problems(lines), one revision's driver lines in, [(probe, problem)] out, where the independent statement disagrees; an exception is a replay that can't be judged, never a violation. runtime.run_controls passes driver_args() and keeps every line the driver prints, its preparation copies the probes file with the oracle, and workflow_ingest reads each revision with problems() against what its pair's kind expects (examples/tools/targets/runtime.py's docstring). Before this, the merged runner looked for a PROBES list and ingestion called check(lines), so the controls could not have run, and check()'s dict would have been read as problems, so a fixed release would have counted as violating. The CLI (`argv`, `check`, the pair comparison) is unchanged.

VF-027 recorded (2026-11-15, example-targets Phase 5, the user's decision): Replay and mutant-replay passed (receipts/replay, receipts/mutant-replay). Every proof task is blocked by an observed capability gap: vulnerable-security, fixed-security and mutant-security stop at the library-interface parameter (WebMvcTags#method's HttpServletRequest); preservation is not executed, since before and after have different dependency closures and jvmcontract's equivalence takes one classpath for both. Each blocked task has an observed blocker in target.json (finding VF-027) and a packet, records/refusals/TASK.json, citing the job that observed it and its receipt (in verification/results/), with the refusal text, the semantics needed, the likely owner module and the closure check; task readiness is blocked. No task is restated over a wrapper or a simpler signature, no expected conclusion changed, and jvmcontract isn't extended in this wave. The reruns predicting each refusal (examples/tools/targets/workflow_refusal.py 285 TASK, which fails on a verdict or any other refusal) are queued as jobs 20261115-005926-example-285-fixed-security-vf-027-rerun, 20261115-005926-example-285-mutant-security-vf-027-rerun, 20261115-005926-example-285-preservation-vf-027-rerun-st, 20261115-005926-example-285-vulnerable-security-vf-027-r.

Closure of the interface-parameter gap queued (2026-11-15, the prove-examples moonshot, item 285): jvmcontract now decides the three security tasks as stated, on the released JARs, with no wrapper. A property check gives WebMvcTags#method's HttpServletRequest an implementation that answers getMethod() (the one accessor the method calls, found by the gap scan's walk) with one String of up to 8 code units, the same on every call, which is the claim's own request model; reads the Tag result through getKey() and getValue(), Strings by content; runs HttpMethod's map of names through a model of java.util.HashMap (HashMap(int), put, get), String.hashCode on content, Objects.requireNonNull in ImmutableTag's constructor, and WebMvcTags' two Pattern.compile calls, whose regular expressions ("//+" and "/$") are plain constants the JDK always compiles; and the gap scan of the fixed release, which ran into its 120 s limit in every earlier attempt, takes 0.04 s. Inline, on the cached JARs and a debug build, the frozen assertion with --nullable request, --gaps strict and --max-array-length 8 was refuted on 2.7.17 (witness HttpServletRequest{getMethod()=""}, result ImmutableTag{key="method", value=""}, replayed in the interpreter and run on a JVM), established on 2.7.18 in 0.1 s, and refuted on the mutant; dropping TRACE or UNKNOWN from the assertion is refuted on 2.7.18 (getMethod()="TRACE"), so the proof is not vacuous. Both predicted blockers were right about what the claim needs (String terms and the map for fixed-security, Pattern.compile in the initializer for vulnerable-security) and each is now implemented, not assumed. These inline runs are no receipts: the tasks' ordinary attempts are queued as jobs 20261115-173146-example-285-vulnerable-security-the-boun, 20261115-173146-example-285-fixed-security-the-bounded-m and 20261115-173146-example-285-mutant-security-the-bounded, and until their receipts decide the unchanged claim 196346d46d4d81fb the three blockers stay recorded in target.json as they are. The refusal reruns (workflow_refusal.py 285 TASK) now fail for these three tasks, as designed when a closure lands. preservation is still blocked on verifier-interface:two-dependency-closures.

Closure of the two-dependency-closures gap queued (2026-11-15, the prove-examples moonshot, item 285): the preservation task can now be attempted as stated, each release on its own pinned closure. jvmcontract's equivalence takes --before-classpath, the previous version's own dependency closure: the previous build is relocated under before/ together with the classes of its closure it names (1,593 of 2.7.17's, 9 MB, under a second), so both releases run in one program and before/io/micrometer/.../ImmutableTag and io/micrometer/.../ImmutableTag are two classes; a class only the new closure has is never the previous version's. examples.title: CVE-2022-22968: Case-sensitive DataBinder disallowedFields
examples.summary: Spring Framework 5.3.18 → 5.3.19, fixed by a7cf19ce: DataBinder matched disallowed field patterns case-sensitively, so a field listed as age could still be bound as Age (the bean wrapper resolves it to age), and one listed as AGE didn't protect age. A deep negative packet: the release pair source-locked, the decision lemma, preservation and the protected-state claim frozen as six tasks, with an oracle, 46 probes, a driver and a mutant; no verifier task has run.
examples.verdictLabel: ✗ a disallowed field allowed through a case alias on 5.3.18 and on the mutant; ✓ denied on 5.3.19 (the decision claim, through its adapter entry, beside the route); ✗ the protected-state claim refuted on 5.3.18, beside the route; preservation and the protected-state claim on 5.3.19 not decided
notes: Pair: the release pair (5.3.18 → 5.3.19, published JARs) is selected. Each release's DataBinder.java is the exact-fix pair's blob (612dfc56, 8ee5e43b, also in the sources JARs), and the decision's helpers (ObjectUtils, PatternMatchUtils, PropertyAccessorUtils) are byte-identical in both closures. The exact-fix pair has no published artifact. The release window's two CachedIntrospectionResults commits change property filters ProtectedBean doesn't reach; the driver prints the resolved properties on each run.

Three claims, kept apart: the decision lemma (claims/disallowed-field-denied-ignoring-case.json, vulnerable-security and fixed-security), preservation outside the case aliases (claims/permitted-fields-preserved.json), and the stronger protected-state claim on the actual binding (claims/protected-age-not-mutated.json, its own vulnerable and fixed tasks), which a decision proof never discharges.

Domain: ASCII names and patterns, a canonical field, and the default locale pinned to Locale.ROOT (the driver sets it before any Spring class loads). Two probes outside it show why: under tr-TR, 5.3.19 lower-cases FAVOURITECOLOUR's I to a dotless i and allows favouriteColour (example 288's locale property); and with the non-ASCII pattern dataΣ*, 5.3.19 lower-cases the pattern's Σ to a final sigma and the field dataΣx's to a medial one, so it allows a field 5.3.18 denies by exact match.

The upstream regression's own value (age=32x) doesn't convert, so on 5.3.18 age stays 0 with a typeMismatch error: that test fails on the suppressed fields only. The probes add the seed's age=32 and the advisory's Age=32, which write the protected age on 5.3.18.

Developer note, not evidence: on 2026-11-14 the stream ran the driver by hand (JARs from Maven Central, hashes as locked) on Temurin 21.0.13 and 25.0.5: 5.3.18 fails the property at exactly the 12 triggers and passes every legitimate probe, 5.3.19 holds and passes, preservation holds with changes only at the triggers and the regression's inputs, and the mutant fails 13 probes with every legitimate one passing; lines identical on both JDKs.

Imported on 2026-11-14 from the archived registry (rank 2, priority P0); its capability notes are from verifier 4c279ba6 and stale. The blockers in target.json are predictions until the capability probe reaches them.

Mutation control as a revision (2026-11-14, example-targets Phase 5): controls/pattern-side-unnormalized.patch is declared in target.json as workflow W1's constructed revision `mutant` (base `fixed-release`, the patch's sha256 locked), the after of the `mutation` pair. It has two tasks of its own: `mutant-replay`, the concrete controls on that pair, where the base must hold and the mutant fail the oracle, and `mutant-security`, fixed-security's claim on the mutant, expected refuted. Its claim is bound to the mutant's artifact (runtime's identity `mutant:<base commit>+<patch sha256>`), never to a release's. It used to be only a `controls` entry on `fixed-release`, which no task prepared.

Could a wrong implementation satisfy the claims? (2026-11-17, the domain-advances challenge stream, item 6.) Yes, all three. controls/first-suppressed-only.patch (sha256 4fddd257…) on 5.3.19 returns from DataBinder.checkAllowedFields after the first value it suppresses, so every later value is bound unchecked. Its isAllowed is the fix's, so disallowed-field-denied-ignoring-case and permitted-fields-preserved are predicted to be decided as on 5.3.19. protected-age-not-mutated binds one value, which the mutant suppresses as the fix does, so it is predicted established. On a JVM with the disallowed pattern AGE, one value Age=32 leaves age 0, but age=5 then Age=32 binds 32 (5.3.19: 0). The probes tell them apart: the oracle reports bind-list-upstream (favouriteColour bound after age was suppressed) and bind-map-upstream (someMap[key4] bound) as security failures. So the replay catches it and no claim does. The protected-state claim would catch it with two property values that both name the protected property (the upstream test binds three). The decision lemma is also satisfied by a binder that denies every field, which is why permitted-fields-preserved exists.

Could a wrong implementation satisfy the proposed two-value claim? (2026-11-18, the domain-advances challenge stream, item 6; the claim is the state stream's claims/proposed/protected-age-kept-two-values.json at its commit kmytvuop, not on every line.) Yes, two, each a patch of 5.3.19's DataBinder.checkAllowedFields under controls/ that no task uses. controls/second-suppressed-last.patch (sha256 ce2b1731…) returns once it has suppressed two values, so a third is bound unchecked. With two values the return comes after the last one, so the claim is predicted established on it, and the frozen claim too; its isAllowed is the fix's, so the decision lemma and permitted-fields-preserved are predicted as on 5.3.19. On a JVM (JDK 25, the pinned 5.3.19 JARs with the patched class first) with AGE disallowed: age=5, Age=32 leaves 0, but aGe=1, AGE=2, Age=32 binds 32 (5.3.19: 0). Only age and Age reach the property (the bean wrapper changes only a name's first unit), and MutablePropertyValues keeps one value per name, so two names that are both denied must come before Age. The replay does not catch it either: the driver's probes on it are 'holds' and 'pass', as on 5.3.19, since no probe binds three denied names. A claim binding k values is met by the mutant that returns after the k-th; one whose names are an array input up to the bound (maxArrayLength 8) is met only past the bound, which it states, and a probe binding aGe, AGE, Age would catch this one. controls/all-dropped-once-suppressed.patch (sha256 1085a14c…) drops every value, permitted ones too, once one is denied: a request that names a disallowed field is refused whole. The claim reads age alone, so it is predicted established, and the frozen claim too; permitted-fields-preserved is about isAllowed, not the binding, so it is predicted as on 5.3.19. On a JVM, name=bob beside Age=32 leaves name null (5.3.19: bob). The replay catches it, with 11 legitimate failures (a permitted value not bound in bind-overlap-upstream, bind-list-upstream, bind-map-upstream and six other probes). No claim says a permitted value beside a denied one is still bound. Both were sent to the state stream, the claim's owner; a new claim is its and the user's.

How the proof finishes (2026-11-15): simpleMatch calls itself at every '*', so unrolled it doubles its paths per character, and comparing it with the claim's regular expression is an equivalence of two matchers. The lemma proofs/simple-match.contract removes both: on ASCII Strings within the bound, simpleMatch(pattern, str) returns what Pattern.compile(String.join(".*", the parts of pattern.split("\\*", -1), each quoted), DOTALL).matcher(str).matches() returns. jvmcontract proves it first, by induction on pattern.length() (prove --lemmas, a `decreases:` line): a recursive call on a shorter pattern within the assumption and the bound is taken to satisfy the lemma, and any other recursive call would end the proof with no verdict. In the decision's proof a call of simpleMatch(String, String) within the lemma's bound and assumption returns what the lemma states, and any other call runs the method as written. The checker holds a quoted, joined and compiled pattern as its pieces, so the lemma's exact match of the lower-cased Strings and the claim's CASE_INSENSITIVE match of the originals (ASCII-only folding, as the JDK's without UNICODE_CASE) are one formula. The regex model is itself checked: proved equal to a matcher written out over charAt at bounds 2 to 4 (lib/tests/claims.rs, fixture R), which agrees with a JVM on 3,000,000 random pairs, U+0130, U+212A and U+017F among them.

Where DataBinder.bind stops, cycle 2 (2026-11-17, the domain-advances state stream). Through the bean wrapper by a stand-in (2026-11-17, the domain-advances state stream, steps 2 and 3). examples.title: CVE-2025-22228: BCryptPasswordEncoder does not enforce maximum password length
examples.summary: Spring Security 6.3.7 → 6.3.8, fixed by 46f0dc6d: BCrypt refuses passwords longer than 72 UTF-8 bytes, which it used to truncate, so a longer candidate authenticated by its 72-byte prefix. A deep negative packet, ready for Phase 5: three frozen claims (the public matches policy, preservation, and a narrower byte-array lemma), an independent oracle, 33 probes against independently made stored hashes, a replay driver and a character-counting mutant. No verifier has run.
examples.verdictLabel: ✗ more than 72 bytes not rejected on 6.3.7 (the guard lemma, by the route; the public claim through its adapter entry, beside the route) and on the mutant; ✓ rejected on 6.3.8 by both; preservation not decided
notes: Execution pair: the release pair, 6.3.7 → 6.3.8 (published-artifact: spring-security-crypto and spring-jcl). It carries the exact fix 36ea1b11 → 46f0dc6d faithfully: each release's BCrypt.java and BCryptPasswordEncoder.java are the exact-fix pair's blobs (0f8d082f, 17292840; d17511b0 in all four), also in the sources JARs, and only BCrypt.hashpw(byte[], String, boolean) differs in the class files (sources.lock.json).

Tasks (target.json): replay; vulnerable-security (expected refuted) and fixed-security (expected established) on claims/overlong-candidate-rejected.json, through example287.adapter.PasswordMatchAdapter (one call of the original matches); preservation (expected established) on claims/in-range-matching-preserved.json outside the allowed change 'a non-null candidate longer than 72 UTF-8 bytes'; vulnerable-guard and fixed-guard, the narrower byte-array lemma on BCrypt.checkpw(byte[], String) (claims/overlong-bytes-rejected.json, relation diagnostic, each with its security task as parent, which it never settles). All native strict.

Domain: a non-null candidate and a valid stored hash (minor a, b or y, cost 04 to 30, 53 base64 characters). Bounds: Strings of up to 80 UTF-16 units, so the rejected branch is reachable (73 bytes take at least 25 units; 8 never reach it). The byte count is the JDK's String.getBytes(UTF_8): an unpaired surrogate becomes one '?' byte. The driver prints the JDK's count for every candidate and the oracle refuses a run where it differs from its own.

Stored hashes are made independently, by pyca bcrypt 5.0.0 from recorded preimages (controls/probes.json's hashes), never by a revision under test and never as matches(overlong, encode(overlong)): upstream's enforcePasswordLength test does that, and passes on the fix because encode throws first.

The oracle (controls/oracle.py) names a violation's kind: authenticated (the advisory's defect), unrejected (an overlong candidate refused with false, not the frozen rejection), wrong-exception, in-range-exception. Its self-test rejects deny-all and reject-all implementations through the legitimate controls and preservation, and checks that probes.json's expectations are each revision's documented shape.

Mutation control: controls/char-count-guard.patch on 6.3.8 counts UTF-16 units instead of bytes (the String entries refuse more than 72 units, and the byte guard is gone). It lets 36 x U+00E9 plus x through (73 bytes, 37 characters).

Developer note, not evidence: by hand with the pinned JARs (sha256 in sources.lock.json) on Temurin 21.0.13 and 25.0.5, 6.3.7 failed at the 12 overlong probes (9 authenticated, 3 unrejected) and passed every legitimate probe; 6.3.8 held and passed; the mutant authenticated the 3 multibyte triggers and the 2 byte-array ones; preservation held, with changes only at the 12; every outcome was the one probes.json wrote before the run, and each revision's lines were identical on both JDKs.

For review: 25 unpaired surrogates authenticate against a hash of 25 '?' on every revision (the JDK's lossy encoding; in range, so not this CVE); a stored hash with cost 31 never terminates for an in-range candidate (an int loop counter against 2^31 rounds, read from the bytecode, not run); and the fix makes a legitimately stored long password unusable, since bcrypt's hash of a 73-byte password is the hash of its first 72 bytes: that is example 300's ground (CVE-2025-22234, 6.3.9's legacy matching).

examples.title: CVE-2024-38820: Locale-sensitive DataBinder case normalization
examples.summary: Spring Framework 6.1.13 → 6.1.14, fixed by 23656aeb: DataBinder lower-cased disallowed field patterns and the field with String.toLowerCase(), the default locale's, so under a Turkish or Azerbaijani default locale a field listed as id could still be bound as Id (I lower-cases to a dotless i), and one listed as ADMIN didn't protect admin. A deep negative packet, set up from its catalog entry: the release pair source-locked, the decision claim in every locale of a stated table and preservation frozen as four proof tasks, with an oracle, 36 probes, a driver and a mutant; both replays pass as expected; no proof task has run.
examples.verdictLabel: replay ✗ on 6.1.13 at the 14 locale triggers, ✓ on 6.1.14, ✗ on the mutant at 8; ✓ the decision claim established on 6.1.14 at the frozen bound (through its adapter entry, beside the route, with the simpleMatch lemma proved by induction); the two refutations and preservation not decided at that bound (VF-031)
notes: Set up from its catalog entry on 2026-11-16 by the setup stage of /prove-java-change (a catalog entry's brief, llm-dlc/runtime.md), with example 286 (CVE-2022-22968, the fix this one corrects) as the model: its decision lemma, assertion and ASCII domain are this packet's, with the default locale made two inputs.

Pair: the release pair (6.1.13 → 6.1.14, published JARs) is selected. Each release's DataBinder.java is the exact-fix pair's blob (c7af62b5, 98157756, also in the sources JARs), and the classes the decision and the bind probes reach besides it (ObjectUtils, PatternMatchUtils, StringUtils, PropertyAccessorUtils, BeanWrapperImpl, AbstractNestablePropertyAccessor, CachedIntrospectionResults, AbstractBindingResult) are byte-identical in both closures (sources.lock.json).

Two claims: the decision claim (claims/disallowed-field-denied-in-every-locale.json: vulnerable-security, fixed-security, mutant-security) and preservation outside the locale-dependent aliases (claims/permitted-fields-preserved.json). No protected-state claim: the bind probes show the alias writing the bean, and the entry's summary asks only for the deny decision.

Locales: the claim's table is the root locale, en-US, tr-TR, az-AZ and lt-LT, entered as two int parameters indexing LocaleDecisionAdapter.LOCALES (the locale while the binder is configured, and while it decides). A sweep run by hand on JDK 21.0.13 and 25.0.5 found tr and az (with their regions and scripts) the only available locales whose String.toLowerCase maps an ASCII letter apart from the root locale's, and only I, to U+0131 (sources.lock.json, locales).

Replay (receipts/replay, 2026-11-16, JDK 21 and 25, identical): 6.1.13 fails the property at exactly the 14 triggers (12 decisions under tr-TR or az-AZ at either moment, and 2 bindings that write the protected id or admin) and passes every legitimate probe; 6.1.14 holds and passes. The mutant replay (receipts/mutant-replay): the mutant fails at 8 probes, each with a capital I in the field decided under tr-TR or az-AZ, and holds where only the configuration is under them.

Repaired on 2026-11-16 (the repair's brief, llm-dlc/runtime.md), as stage 2's plan for the run asked: (1) controls/oracle.py's canonical() was a regular expression needing two quote characters, so it left ['] as it is where Spring's PropertyAccessorUtils.canonicalPropertyName gives ] (a key of one quote character both starts and ends with it: Spring deletes the quote, then the [ now before the ]). It is now a transcription of Spring's loop, checked on a JVM against canonicalPropertyName of 6.1.13 and 6.1.14 on JDK 21 and 25 for 3928 Strings (null, every String of at most 5 characters over [ ] ' " a, and every String of the probes): no disagreement, where the regular expression disagreed on 146. The self-test holds 13 of those shapes (CANONICAL_SHAPES). No probe of the first 36 had such a shape, so their verdicts are unchanged. (2) Two guarded probes, one-single-quote-key-root and one-double-quote-key-root: patterns ['] and ["], field ], both moments under the root locale, no allowed list. Both releases and the mutant deny ], as the claim's predicate says. (3) Both replays ran again over the 38 probes (receipts/replay/20261116T193627Z-070b6fac, receipts/mutant-replay/20261116T193635Z-b90da1c3, which replace the two of the setup): the 14 triggers and the mutant's 8 are unchanged, and the comparison is preserved, with 15 changes inside the allowed region. (4) claims/permitted-fields-preserved.json: the statement said more than the page and the task. It also said which answer the releases give, which an equivalence does not show. It now states agreement only, as the plan's 'misstates' remark gave it word for word, and the remark's note on the expected answers is added to the claim's notes. Its assume, assumptions, allowed change, bounds and domain are unchanged. (5) Each proof task records how it is invoked (target.json, invocation).

Queued at the frozen bound beside the route (2026-11-16, the proof loop of /prove-java-change): no verdict at bound 8 yet. proofs/prove.py runs each frozen claim, unchanged, through the adapter entry its first assumption names (LocaleDecisionAdapter#allowed), on each revision's pinned JARs. What the verifier gained for it: (1) the default locale as state the own checker follows (lib/src/bmc/locale.rs): Locale's constants, Locale.forLanguageTag of a constant plain tag, Locale.setDefault, and String.toLowerCase() and toLowerCase(Locale) on ASCII under a locale that is an input, with Turkish and Azeri lowering I to U+0131; (2) a reference read from an array at a computed index is one symbolic reference among the cells, so the two locale indices split no path; (3) a regression check over String[] parameters, an assumption and lemmas is made as a property of the pair of versions (lib/src/pairing.rs), each release on its own class path. Inline probes at small bounds gave every expected verdict: fixed-security established at 2 (0.9 s) and 5 (47 s); vulnerable-security refuted at 3 in 8 s on allowed(configLocale=0, bindLocale=2, allowedPatterns={"*", "", ""}, disallowedPatterns={null, null, "**I"}, field="I"); mutant-security refuted at 3 in 5 s on allowed(configLocale=0, bindLocale=2, allowedPatterns={"*\u0013[", null, "*"}, disallowedPatterns={"[*i", "[[]"}, field="[[I"), both witnesses under a tr-TR decision-time default and run on a JVM (JDK 25.0.5); preservation established at 2, 3 and 4 (48 s at 4), and refuted at 2 when given no allowed change, which shows the check sees the change. Jobs: 20261116-201436-example-288-fixed-security-through-the-a, 20261116-201436-example-288-vulnerable-security-through, 20261116-201436-example-288-mutant-security-through-the, 20261116-203637-example-288-preservation-through-the-ada. A probe at a small bound is not the claim's verdict: the verdict label stays 'not run' until the jobs report.

For review, outside the claims' ASCII domain: the bind probe bind-dotted-capital-i-root shows the field İd (U+0130, capital I with a dot) writing the protected id against the pattern id on both releases, under the root locale: String.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT) gives i followed by U+0307, which the pattern doesn't match, while the bean wrapper's fallback lookup (StringUtils.uncapitalize, Character.toLowerCase) resolves İd to id. And under tr-TR 6.1.13 denies İd (it lower-cases to id there) where 6.1.14 allows it. Neither is part of a claim.
