Revisions checked against upstream on 2026-11-14, and again on 2026-11-16 for the setup: the release tags resolved to commits, each fix commit and its parent read from github.com, and the fix an ancestor of the fixed release and not of the vulnerable one.
Proof boundary (research): a locale-invariance theorem is separate from case-insensitive protection. The 2022 parent may satisfy the former while violating the latter; never call it generally secure.

Feasibility (research): requires honest String/Locale models; a solver stub treating all toLowerCase calls identically would conceal this CVE. The mutant is the check on that: it differs from 6.1.14 only where the field is lower-cased under tr-TR or az-AZ.

What binding writes, under the table's locales (2026-11-17, the state stream's step 6: the second consumer of the permitted setters' effect contracts, example 286's proofs/beans/protected-setters.contract being the first). proofs/beans/example288/adapter/ProtectedBinding#protectedKept binds one property value {field, value} onto a fresh ProtectedBean with id and admin disallowed by "id" and "ADMIN", the binder configured under LOCALES[configLocale] and binding under LOCALES[bindLocale], and returns whether id is 0 and admin false. proofs/beans.py runs it on each release through the bean wrapper's stand-in (proofs/beans/org/springframework/beans/ProtectedBeanStandIn.java, sampled against the release's setPropertyValue(PropertyValue): 741,600 samples under the five locales, all equal on 6.1.13 and 6.1.14) and the effect contracts of setName and setTitle (proofs/beans/protected-setters.contract: each writes its own field only and leaves the String it is given), with example 286's models and observed initializers, over ASCII simple names and any value, at bound 8. In capped probes 6.1.14 is proved (86 s, 830 MB), resting on the two contracts and the stand-in, and 6.1.13 is refuted at protectedKept(configLocale=2, bindLocale=2, field="Id", value="-9"), run on a JVM. The contracts carried over as 286's are, the class aside: they are applied under a default locale the path set (tr-TR, az-AZ), since their proofs read nothing that was there before the call, the default locale included. What was particular to 286 was the stand-in's lookup: there only A to Z lower-case to a property's first unit, here U+0130 also lowers to id's i (the bind-dotted-capital-i-root finding), which the sweep of every first unit shows (785 samples differ without it). Job 20261117-235132 ran both checks at bound 8 and gave both expected answers: proved on 6.1.14 in 5.7 s after the stand-in's sampling and the contracts' proofs, refuted on 6.1.13 with the witness run on a JVM (2 min 59 s in all, peak 2.6 GiB). None of it is a task of target.json or in the adapter set, and neither claim is changed.

The simpleMatch lemma under the tightened lemma checks (2026-11-17). The checker's rule for a lemma (prove --lemmas) now refuses a lemma whose method or expressions read a static field that is not final, a non-final field or array cell of an object that was there before the call, or the default locale, and holds a method proved by induction to the write checks. Job 20261117-122546-examples-286-and-288-the-simplematch-lem reran fixed-security at the frozen bound with the lemma under those checks (into verification/.work-288/tightened): the lemma is still proved by induction on pattern.length() (108.5 s), and fixed-security is verified with it (1037.5 s, 4678 paths), so the earlier result did not rest on the hole and nothing was refused.

Recorded beside the route (2026-11-17, the evidence stream). fixed-security had one verified run (job 20261116-201436-example-288-fixed-security-through-the-a) whose driver recorded nothing of what it ran, so it was never recorded as an answer. Job 20261117-133148-example-288-fixed-security-again-with-th reran it unchanged at the frozen bound through the shared driver module (examples/tools/beside_route.py), into verification/.work-288/recorded: passed in 20m39s at 1.4 GiB, the simpleMatch lemma proved by induction on pattern.length() in 106.0 s under the tightened lemma checks, and fixed-security verified in 1130.9 s (4678 paths, 8753 solver calls), not vacuous at allowed(configLocale=4, bindLocale=4, allowedPatterns=null, disallowedPatterns=null, field=""). The task's besideRoute names that job, and python3 examples/tools/accept.py 288 accepts it with no limit: the outcome is the one the step wrote, its expressions the frozen claim's, at bound 8 with strict gaps, complete, and the 4 JARs, the adapter sources and the claim the driver recorded (evidence.json) the ones target.json pins, the verifier's binary recorded (sha256 14673718…). What it rests on besides the checker's own assumptions: the simpleMatch lemma, proved beside it at the same bounds and applied at its calls within the lemma's ASCII domain. The verdict label now names this one answer; vulnerable-security, mutant-security and preservation are still undecided at the frozen bound (VF-031).

preservation profiled (2026-11-17/18, the preservation stream, step 7 of domain-advances-preservation.md; no claim, bound or driver argument changed). Capped probes on today's checker, the frozen claim at maxArrayLength 8 (--timeout 160): the lemmas are proved first (69 s and 23 s), then the pair runs out of time with about 4100 paths, 8700 solver calls and 1.8 million variables, 136 of its 160 s in the solver. A temporary log of every solver call by the frames it was asked from (removed) showed where that time goes. First, configuring the binder: PropertyAccessorUtils.canonicalPropertyName (spring-beans, the same bytecode in both releases) over each allowed and disallowed pattern, run by the allowed change's scope, by 6.1.13 and by 6.1.14, takes about 72 of the 136 s (each probe some 40 ms at that size). The matcher (simpleMatch through the lemma) takes under 3 s, and the locale table forks little. Second, the end: trials at smaller bounds show the cost growing steeply with the length of the Strings and arrays (verified in 13 s at 3 and in 42 s at 4, undecided after 150 s at 5 and 6). At 4, the most expensive call is the last, RegressionPair.agree's comparison of the two releases' results (5.6 s probed, then 15.9 s decided), so VF-031's 1h32m most likely ended in that query at 8. It is relational: outside the allowed change, a disallowed pattern may hold a capital I configured under tr-TR or az-AZ yet match the field in no case. The two releases' lower-cased patterns then differ (U+0131 against i), and only reasoning about both matches shows that neither matches. Tried and not kept: relating the two releases' applications of the simpleMatch lemma by their inputs, as the one-function rule relates its calls (the same code on equal inputs gives one result). It related 154 of 309 applications at bound 4 and left the time where it was (46 s; the final query 17 s), because the hard case is the one whose inputs differ. Without the lemma, the one-function rule takes 826 simpleMatch calls at bound 4 and does not finish in 150 s. What would address the hard case is a fact about each release alone that the pair can use, such as a lemma over the matcher of lower-cased Strings: simpleMatch(lower(p), lower(f)) under the claim's locales implies that p matches f ignoring ASCII case, so a pattern that matches in no case matches in neither release. That is the next approach; no job was queued, since a job at the frozen bound on today's checker would repeat VF-031.

Could a wrong implementation satisfy the claims? (2026-11-18, the domain-advances challenge stream, item 6.) The run decides one answer here: fixed-security, the decision claim established on 6.1.14 (job 20261116-201436-example-288-fixed-security-through-the-a, again in 20261117-133148), with both refutations; preservation is unverifiable at bound 8 (the solver's time limit, VF-031). Two wrong 6.1.14 binders satisfy what is decided, each a patch of 6.1.14's DataBinder.java under controls/ that no task uses. controls/allowed-list-skipped-with-disallowed.patch (sha256 3fbc5f84…) consults the allowed list only when no disallowed list is set: with both set, a field the allowed list leaves out is bound. The decision claim reads the disallowed side alone, and the mutant's disallowed side is the fix's, so fixed-security is predicted established on it: with a disallowed list set its result is exactly the fix's disallowed conjunct, which the fix's proof covers on its inputs with allowedPatterns null. The preservation claim tells it apart (Name against the allowed list name, with id disallowed, under the root locale, is outside the allowed change: 6.1.13 denies, the mutant allows), but it is the claim with no verdict. On a JVM (JDK 25.0.5, the pinned 6.1.14 JARs with the patched class first), allowed name, disallowed id, name=Ayla, title=Dr binds title Dr (6.1.14: title suppressed). The replay catches it, at one legitimate probe (name-capital-allowed-list-tr: Name allowed, the statement says denied), and holds the property. controls/first-suppressed-only.patch (sha256 f5eea9ce…) is example 286's mutant of the same name on this release: checkAllowedFields returns after the first suppressed value. Its isAllowed is the fix's, so all three decision tasks are predicted as on 6.1.14. The state stream's binding check (proofs/beans.py, ProtectedBinding#protectedKept, commit ownxunnx, job 20261117-235132, no task) binds one value {field, value}, so on it the return comes where the loop ends anyway, and it is predicted established at bound 8 as on 6.1.14. On a JVM with id and ADMIN disallowed: id=5, Id=7 binds id 7, and admin=false, Admin=true makes an admin (6.1.14: both suppressed); one value is kept out, as the check says. The replay misses it too: 'holds' and 'pass', as on 6.1.14, since no bind probe has two denied names. The limit is 286's, reported there (domain-advances-state-I009 and I019): a check of k values is met by the binder that stops after the k-th. So the decided answer says that the deny decision is right, not that the binder protects the bean: this packet states as much (the decision only; no protected-state claim), and the two halves it leaves to other evidence are the allowed list (preservation, unverified; one probe) and the binding of more than one value (no claim, no probe). The first went to the preservation stream, which owns 288's preservation task, and the second to the state stream, which owns the binding check.

examples.title: CVE-2022-22978: Authorization bypass in RegexRequestMatcher
examples.summary: Spring Security 5.6.3 → 5.6.4, fixed by 70863952: RegexRequestMatcher compiled its pattern without Pattern.DOTALL, so the '.' of a protective rule such as /admin/.* didn't match a line terminator, and a request whose servlet path a container had decoded to /admin/ followed by a line feed escaped the rule. A deep negative packet, set up from its catalog entry: the release pair source-locked, the security claim (a literal prefix and '.*' matches every URL that begins with the prefix, line terminators included, in either case mode) and preservation frozen as four proof tasks, with an oracle, 44 probes, a request carrier, a driver and a mutant; both replays pass as expected; the four proof tasks are decided at the frozen bound beside the route, through the adapter entry: the security claim refuted on 5.6.3 and on the mutant, established on 5.6.4, and preservation established.
examples.verdictLabel: ✗ a URL in the protected namespace with a line terminator unmatched on 5.6.3 and, case-insensitively, on the mutant; ✓ matched on 5.6.4, and 5.6.3 and 5.6.4 agree outside that change (both claims, through the adapter entry, beside the route)
notes: Set up from its catalog entry on 2026-11-16 by the setup stage of /prove-java-change (a catalog entry's brief, llm-dlc/runtime.md), with examples 285 (its request carrier) and 288 (the packet's shape) as the models.

Decided beside the route (2026-11-16, the proof loop of /prove-java-change): each of the four proof tasks has its expected verdict at the frozen bound (maxArrayLength 8, --engine native --gaps strict, loops followed for 26 turns), run by proofs/prove.py on each revision's pinned JARs with the adapter and carrier compiled against them. fixed-security (job 20261116-214343-example-289-fixed-security-through-the-a): established on 5.6.4 over a pattern, a servlet path, a path info and a query of at most 8 code units each (the last two or null) and both case modes, in 36 s (1,003 paths, 322,652 variables, 1,231,598 clauses, 265 MiB peak), not vacuous. vulnerable-security (job 20261116-214344-example-289-vulnerable-security-through): refuted on 5.6.3 in 2 s at matches(pattern=".*", caseInsensitive=false, servletPath="", pathInfo="\u07ff\ufea0\u2028", query=null), which returns false: the URL begins with the empty prefix and holds a line separator. mutant-security (job 20261116-214344-example-289-mutant-security-through-the): refuted on the constructed mutant in 2 s at matches(pattern=".*", caseInsensitive=true, servletPath="\ufea0\ufea0\ufea0\ufea0\ufea0", pathInfo="\u2029\ufea0\ufea0\ufea0", query=null), which returns false, through caseInsensitive true as expected; the mutant prove.py builds is byte for byte the JAR the mutant replay ran (sha256 a3a3dbff86c1…). Each witness was run in the harness on a JVM (JDK 25.0.5), where the release's bytecode and Java's own java.util.regex decide it. preservation (job 20261116-214344-example-289-preservation-through-the-ada): established on the release pair in 61 s (1,373 paths, 415,833 variables, 1,574,995 clauses, 551 MiB peak): outside a URL that begins with the prefix and holds a line terminator, 5.6.3 and 5.6.4 return the same value; given no allowed change, a probe refuted the pair at bound 3 on a URL holding U+2028. Nothing is put in a method's place and no lemma is given: the constructor and matches run as written, so the flags are the ones each release computes. The verifier gained one guarded rule for it (lib/src/bmc/regex.rs): Pattern.compile(String, int) of a String that is an input is modelled only where the solver shows that on the path it can only be characters that stand for themselves followed by '.*'; the Pattern is then those characters as a quoted text and '.' any number of times, and any other pattern stays the JDK's call, refused by name. The two flags are formulas (the constructor chooses them by caseInsensitive), and one '.*' at an expression's end takes unpaired surrogates, where matching by unit is the JDK's matching by code point. Beside it: Character.isLetter of an ASCII char and IntStream.range, which the claim's own expression calls, and Logger.isLoggable below INFO as false under a stated assumption (the matcher's debug line goes through spring-jcl to java.util.logging; the claim's fourth assumption). Each rule is proved to be its definition written out in Java on every input of a bound, and the definition sampled against the JDK on a JVM (lib/tests/claims.rs, claims.P and claims.Samples). Two things a reader of the proofs should know. The checks follow loops for 26 turns, not the checker's default 16: the allowed change reads the URL unit by unit and the URL is up to 25 units (three Strings of 8 and a '?'); at 16 a probe of preservation covered the loop by an invariant, found a state no run reaches, ran it on a JVM, and reported no verdict. And the claim's expressions were compared with the oracle before any proof (proofs/predicates.py): compiled by javac and run on a JVM, they read all 44 probes as controls/oracle.py does. What the verdicts do not say: nothing about patterns outside the family (the probes dot-inside-pattern and inline-flag-turns-dotall-off), Strings longer than 8 code units, a JVM with java.util.logging configured to log FINE for the matcher, the firewall or the filter chain. They are proofs beside the route, not route receipts.

Pair: the release pair (5.6.3 → 5.6.4, published JARs) is selected. Each release's RegexRequestMatcher.java is the exact-fix pair's blob (9264b56f, a334afc7, also in the sources JARs), and the classes the matcher reaches besides it (StringUtils, LogMessage and its nested classes, HttpMethod, all of spring-jcl) are byte-identical in the two closures, Spring Framework 5.3.19 and 5.3.20 (sources.lock.json).

The release pair holds one more change: StrictHttpFirewall rejects non-printable characters in the servlet path and path info, where 5.6.3 checks the request URI alone (whose %0a is printable). It came in a commit before the fix (the fix's parent already has 5.6.4's StrictHttpFirewall.java, blob cb24811f), and it is outside the matcher: behind the strict firewall a 5.6.4 filter chain rejects these requests before any matcher, which is not part of a claim.

Two claims: the security claim (claims/protected-prefix-matched-across-line-terminators.json: vulnerable-security, fixed-security, mutant-security) and preservation outside a URL in the protected namespace holding a line terminator (claims/prefix-classification-preserved.json). Narrowest reading of the entry: the matcher's classification for a literal prefix and '.*', with no HTTP method (as regexMatchers(String...) builds a rule), in either case mode; the chain's fallback rule, the firewall and other patterns are outside, named in the claims' notes.

Entry: example289.adapter.RegexMatchAdapter#matches(String pattern, boolean caseInsensitive, String servletPath, String pathInfo, String query), which builds the original matcher and asks it of example289.carrier.PathOnlyRequest, an HttpServletRequest supplying those three getters as given and throwing on every other servlet method (example 285's carrier, its overrides reused). Neither release reads anything else of the request.

Replay (receipts/replay, 2026-11-16, JDK 21 and 25, identical, rerun with the surrogate probes, the matcher's logger reporting debug off): 5.6.3 fails the property at exactly the 18 triggers (\n, \r, CR LF, U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029 after the prefix, in the servlet path, the path info or the query, and a line feed after an unpaired high surrogate, for both constructors, the upstream tests' two among them) and passes every guarded and legitimate probe; 5.6.4 holds and passes; the comparison is preserved, every change inside the allowed region. The mutant replay (receipts/mutant-replay): the mutant fails at exactly the 5 case-insensitive triggers and holds elsewhere.

For review, outside the claims' domain: on 5.6.4 a pattern with an inline (?-s) still misses /admin/ followed by a line feed (probe inline-flag-turns-dotall-off): the fix sets DOTALL as a default the pattern can turn off. A '.' with more pattern after it (/files/.*\.txt, probe dot-inside-pattern) changes from unmatched to matched as the claims' family does. A null servlet path throws NullPointerException on both.

Unpaired surrogates, which the claims' domain includes (probes added on 2026-11-16, as the /prove-java-change plan's review asked): a lone high surrogate (U+D800) after /admin/, a lone low one (U+DC00), and a pair split between the servlet path (U+D83D) and the path info (U+DE00), each in both case modes, are matched by both releases and the mutant; /admin/ then U+D800 then a line feed is a trigger like the others, unmatched on 5.6.3, matched on 5.6.4, and missed by the mutant in the case-insensitive mode. The driver prints each probe's strings as their UTF-16 code units, so the route's controls record (runtime.run_controls, which writes the parsed observations as UTF-8 and couldn't hold a lone surrogate) holds them as ASCII. Its first line also reports whether the matcher's logger has debug enabled and whether a java.util.logging configuration property is set, and the oracle refuses a run with debug on or unreported: the claims assume the debug line is not logged.

Imported on 2026-11-14 from the archived registry (llm-dlc/loops/example-targets-inputs/spring-cve-targets.research-2026-11-04.json, as of 2026-11-04, rank 5, priority P1). Its capability notes are from verifier 4c279ba6 and stale; the blockers in target.json are predictions, with one more predicted from example 286's observed refusals (preservation's two closures, and the route's missing adapter entry).

Revisions checked against upstream on 2026-11-14, and again on 2026-11-16 for the setup: the release tags resolved to commits, each fix commit and its parent read from github.com, and the fix an ancestor of the fixed release and not of the vulnerable one.

Proof boundary (research): matcher classification depends on JDK regex behaviour and the servlet path's representation; proving that the flag equals Pattern.DOTALL is not an authorization theorem. The claims quantify over the pattern's prefix, the case mode and every request string, so java.util.regex is on the proof's path, not a constant.
Feasibility (research): Medium. Small code delta, but the property depends on java.util.regex.Pattern semantics; the mutant is the check that a proof doesn't fix the case-sensitive constructor.

The acceptance check (2026-11-17, examples/tools/accept.py; `python3 examples/tools/accept.py 289`). The four answers beside the route are accepted from their saved results, by the checks an outside review made by hand on 2026-11-16: each outcome is the file its job's step wrote, at bound 8 with strict gaps, its expressions the frozen claim's, preservation's allowed change the one in the generated pair, both refutations reproduced on a JVM, both establishments complete with a witness that reaches the property, and the mutant's JAR (sha256 a3a3dbff…) the one the mutant replay ran. One limit is left on each: the jobs recorded no identity of the JARs, the compiled adapter or the verifier's binary. proofs/prove.py now writes evidence.json beside each outcome with those, ends the run when the mutant's JAR is not the replay's (it only printed the two hashes before), and marks a run at another bound a trial. Job 20261117-122454-example-289-the-four-proof-tasks-again-w reran the four tasks with it into verification/.work-289/recorded (passed in 1m33s, the same four verdicts, on the checker after its soundness fixes of 2026-11-17); each task's besideRoute names that job since 2026-11-17, and accept.py accepts all four from it with no limit: every JAR of each class path is the one target.json pins (the mutant's, but for its own JAR, its base's), the adapter's sources the ones it compiled, and the verifier's binary recorded (sha256 14673718…). The first run of the check refused mutant-security: the driver records the mutant's class path under the revision `mutant`, and the check looked the base's JARs up under that revision, where target.json pins none; the check now looks a constructed mutant's JARs up under its base.

Vacuity outside the allowed change (2026-11-17, the evidence stream's step 4). The pair's `agree` returns true on an input inside the allowed change without calling either version, and the property check's probe asked only for an input of the assumption, so the statement's witness could lie inside the change and a proof that compared nothing was called non-vacuous. The control, run as a capped probe through this example's own driver with only the allowed change replaced by `true`: the checker verified preservation and called it non-vacuous (witness pattern=".*", servletPath of eight U+FEA0), on the engine before the fix. The fix (lib/src/pairing.rs) checks `meantToChange` against `result` over the same assumption: now the `true` run is vacuous, and the run with the task's own allowed change is non-vacuous with the witness agree(pattern=".*", caseInsensitive=true, servletPath="", pathInfo="", query=""), which the outcome says lies outside the change (`stated.vacuity.outside`; 0.3 s more). accept.py now refuses an establishment of a task with an allowed change whose outcome does not say so, so this example's accepted preservation (job 20261117-122454) is refused until a run of a checker with the fix answers it. The standing control is lib/tests/pairing.rs a_pairs_proof_is_vacuous_when_the_allowed_change_covers_every_assumed_input.

2026-11-17, the challenge stream (domain-advances, item 1): the accepted preservation result is the pair of versions' (lib/src/pairing.rs), which compares an exception by its category in harness::EXCEPTIONS, not its class, while the claim says 'throw the same exception'. Two unrelated RuntimeExceptions outside the list, or an IllegalArgumentException and a subclass of it, 'agree' there (countermodels in lib/tests/fixtures/pairing-countermodels, proved to agree though a JVM tells them apart). So the result says less than its claim on any input of the domain where both releases throw different classes of one category; whether there is such an input is not shown. Not affected by the pair's other holes: the run passes --before-classpath (no library static shared), its allowed change calls no code of either release, and the adapter sets no default locale. Open until the preservation stream's pairing compares exceptions by class and the task is rerun; the record is the challenge brief's Progress.

2026-11-17, the challenge stream (domain-advances, item 5, after the preservation stream's wokytpkz): the pair of versions now compares an exception by its class's name and the names of the classes above it up to Object, which answers the item 1 note above. What it does not compare is the rest of what a caller's handler can read of an exception: the interfaces its class implements, its message, and its own fields. lib/tests/fixtures/thrown-pair-countermodels has three pairs, each proved to agree with no stated assumption where a handler tells the versions apart on a JVM. Could a wrong implementation satisfy this claim? A release that throws the same class with another message, or with another interface or field, satisfies the claim as the pair reads it. In this example's pinned JARs, no class named *Exception or *Error differs between the releases in what it extends, what it implements, or its members (javap -p), so the interface and field cases cannot occur here. Whether a message differs on the domain was not checked. The claim's 'the same exception' is one class name and one chain of superclass names, and it should say so, or the pair should compare the message too (sent to the preservation stream).

Preservation accepted again (2026-11-18, the preservation stream, by the user's D036). The task record now names job 20261117-213024-examples-289-and-290-preservation-again, step 1, which reran preservation at the frozen bound 8 into verification/.work-289/closed-fields: verified, 1373 paths, unwinding 26 complete, its witness agree(pattern=".*", caseInsensitive=true, servletPath="", pathInfo="", query="") outside the allowed change. `accept.py 289` accepts it with 13 checks and no recorded limit; the older job's outcome lacked vacuity.outside, which accept.py now asks of a preservation answer. The pair compares an exception by its class's name, the interfaces it implements and the names of the classes above it up to Object, gives each version its own copies of the array arguments, and checks the allowed change on inputs outside it (vacuity.outside); an exception's message, cause and own fields are not compared, as the challenge stream's item 5 note above says. The checker was at source commit 6d515865 (the observer's absolute log path, the reach resolving each field to its declaring class); JDK 25.0.5. The one-function rule's side conditions (I023, later) do not bear on this result: no call was taken as one function of both versions here, and a capped probe after them verified it again.

Could a wrong implementation satisfy the claims? (2026-11-18, the domain-advances challenge stream, item 6; the preservation answer's entry is the note above.) The decided answers here are fixed-security and preservation, both established, and two refutations. On the claims' family (a literal prefix P of ASCII letters, digits, '/', '-' and '_', then '.*') and at bound 8, the two established claims together fix 5.6.4's answer on every input: where the URL begins with P the security claim says true, and anywhere else the preservation claim says 5.6.3's answer. So a wrong 5.6.4 can satisfy both only by differing outside that domain. Two do, each a patch of 5.6.4's RegexRequestMatcher.java (blob a334afc7, checked) under controls/ that no task uses. controls/dotall-for-trailing-wildcard-only.patch (sha256 0dd0654b…) sets DOTALL only for a pattern that ends with '.*', as a fix of the advisory's one example might. Every pattern of the family ends so, so fixed-security and preservation are predicted established on it as on 5.6.4. controls/query-dropped.patch (sha256 5bb6666a…) matches against servletPath + pathInfo and leaves the query out. P cannot hold '?', so on the family the query never decides whether the URL begins with P, and with DOTALL set '.*' takes whatever follows. Both claims are predicted established on it too. On a JVM (JDK 25.0.5, the pinned 5.6.4 JARs with the patched class first), 5.6.4 gives true in each case below, and so does 5.6.3 for the last one. The first mutant misses '/admin/.*/edit' at /admin/ then a line feed then /edit, and '/files/.*\.txt' at /files/a, a line feed, .txt. That is the advisory's bypass, for a '.' with more pattern after it. The second mutant misses '/files/.*\?download=.*' for servlet path /files/a with query download=1, so a rule written on the query never matches. The replay cannot tell either from the fix: each holds and passes on the 44 probes, and oracle.py compare against 5.6.3 finds them preserved, with changes only inside the allowed region. The first mutant differs from 5.6.4 only at the out-of-domain probe dot-inside-pattern (false where 5.6.4 says true), which the oracle reports apart and which decides nothing. No probe's pattern reads the query. The two refutations (vulnerable-security and mutant-security) are answers about a given implementation, and each witness was run on a JVM. No wrong implementation can stand in for them. The packet states the family's narrowness (claims' second assumption, and 'nothing about patterns outside the family' above). What it does not say is what that narrowness leaves out: the fix's effect on every other pattern with a '.', and the query's role in the URL. Making dot-inside-pattern a decided probe, or adding a probe whose pattern reads the query, would catch each mutant. Sent to the preservation stream, which reran this example's preservation.

examples.title: CVE-2023-34035: Authorization rules can be misconfigured when using multiple servlets
examples.summary: Spring Security 5.8.4 → 5.8.5, fixed by df239b64: requestMatchers(String...) and requestMatchers(HttpMethod, String...) chose MvcRequestMatchers whenever Spring MVC was on the class path, so in an application that registers the DispatcherServlet beside other servlets a rule meant for another servlet's paths was matched with Spring MVC's semantics. 5.8.5 looks at the servlet registrations and rejects that configuration with IllegalArgumentException. A deep negative packet, set up from its catalog entry: the release pair source-locked, the security claim (more than one servlet registered, one of them the DispatcherServlet: both implicit overloads throw IllegalArgumentException) and preservation (the DispatcherServlet alone keeps its selection) frozen as four proof tasks, with an oracle, 29 probes, carriers for the context, the servlet context and the registrations, a driver and a mutant; both replays pass as expected; no proof task has run.
examples.verdictLabel: ✗ the security claim refuted on 5.8.4 and on the mutant, ✓ established on 5.8.5, and ✓ the lone DispatcherServlet's selection preserved from 5.8.4 to 5.8.5, each at the frozen bound (through the adapter entry, beside the route; library initializers observed on a JVM and a model of ArrayList run on request, as each outcome states)
notes: Set up from its catalog entry on 2026-11-16 by the setup stage of /prove-java-change (a catalog entry's brief, llm-dlc/runtime.md), from the plan's entry for it (claims, controls and entry designed by stage 2), with examples 285 (carriers for servlet interfaces), 287 (expected outcomes per revision in the probes) and 289 (the packet's shape) as the models. Last in the run's order: the claim is short and the fix a dozen lines, but the method's inputs are an application context, a servlet registry and the class path, which no earlier example gave the verifier.

Pair: the release pair (5.8.4 → 5.8.5, published JARs) is selected. Each release's AbstractRequestMatcherRegistry.java is the exact-fix pair's blob (9760353c, 0df4204d, also in the sources JARs). Of the other classes the replays load from the two closures (Spring Framework 5.3.28 and 5.3.29), all are byte-identical but HandlerMappingIntrospector and AbstractApplicationContext (the same code once constant-pool indexes are masked), Environment (methods in another order) and LogFactory (5.3.29 adds deprecated methods; getLog is the same): sources.lock.json. No class of spring-aop, spring-expression or spring-security-crypto loads, so the closures leave them out.

Two claims, written as the plan designed them: the security claim (claims/ambiguous-servlet-configuration-rejected.json: vulnerable-security, fixed-security, mutant-security) and selection preservation with the DispatcherServlet alone (claims/lone-dispatcher-selection-preserved.json). Narrowest reading of the entry: rejection in the ambiguous configuration, about the DispatcherServlet class itself beside loadable servlet classes on one flat class path, and the configuration's decision only, not what a matcher lets through at request time.

Known gap between the claims (the plan's): a registry that rejects the ambiguous configurations and chooses MvcRequestMatchers everywhere else passes both. The oracle fails it, because it asserts AntPathRequestMatchers on 5.8.5 where no DispatcherServlet is registered (the upstream test requestMatchersWhenNoDispatcherServletThenAntPathRequestMatcherType); no claim states that selection, which would be wider than the advisory and is the user's to add.

Entry: example290.adapter.MatcherSelectionAdapter#select(int[] servlets, int method, String[] patterns). It builds a LinkedHashMap of registrations named servlet0, servlet1, … from a table of class names (0 DispatcherServlet, 1 the packet's PlainServlet, 2 its ExtendedDispatcherServlet, 3 a name no loader holds), puts it in carriers (example290.carrier: RegistryContext, a WebApplicationContext; RegistrationsServletContext; NamedRegistration; PassThroughPostProcessor) and a fresh SelectionRegistry (the three abstract methods implemented, nothing else overridden), then makes one call of the original overload: requestMatchers(patterns) for method -1, requestMatchers(HttpMethod.values()[method], patterns) for 0 to 7. It returns 1000 per MvcRequestMatcher plus 1 per AntPathRequestMatcher, or -1 for another class. Each carrier method outside the four answers throws, naming itself; no release reached one. The carriers' generated overrides were made by reflection from the interfaces of the two closures (identical in both).

javap on every class of both spring-security-config JARs: no class but AbstractRequestMatcherRegistry declares requestMatchers(String...) or requestMatchers(HttpMethod, String...); the configuration DSL's seven registries inherit both, so the minimal subclass runs the same bytecode they do (the plan's assumption, confirmed).

Replay (receipts/replay, 2026-11-16, JDK 21 and 25, identical): 5.8.4 fails the property at all 12 ambiguous probes (it returns MvcRequestMatchers: 1000 or 2000, or 0 with no pattern) and the no-DispatcherServlet assertion, and passes the lone-DispatcherServlet and explicit probes; 5.8.5 holds and passes everything; every outcome is the one probes.json wrote for that revision before the run. The comparison is preserved: 16 changes, all inside the allowed region, none on the lone DispatcherServlet. The mutant replay (receipts/mutant-replay; mutant JAR sha256 4ee35d0bb11b…): the mutant fails at exactly the 6 ambiguous probes whose first registration is the plain servlet and whose patterns are non-null, and agrees with 5.8.5 elsewhere.

Beyond the plan's probes, three with a null pattern element (the domain includes null elements): on the mutant, servlets {1, 0} with patterns {"/a/**", null} throws IllegalArgumentException from AntPathRequestMatcher's Assert.hasText, not from a rejection, so it satisfies the claim's throws clause for another reason: the mutant's counterexamples need patterns with no null or empty element (the plan's least witness, no pattern, is one). And with no DispatcherServlet registered, 5.8.5 throws the same Ant IllegalArgumentException for a null pattern where 5.8.4 returned an MvcRequestMatcher (inside the allowed change). MvcRequestMatcher's constructor takes a null pattern without a check: with the DispatcherServlet alone, every revision returns one for {null}.

For review, outside the claims' domain (observed as the source predicts): 5.8.5 counts a DispatcherServlet subclass as a DispatcherServlet (alone: MvcRequestMatchers; beside a plain servlet, either order: rejected). It stops looking at the first registration whose class can't be loaded: an unloadable class before the DispatcherServlet ({3, 0}) gives AntPathRequestMatchers with no error, after it ({0, 3}) a rejection. On this flat class path that is an observation about order, not evidence of a deployed configuration that can be exploited.

The oracle (controls/oracle.py) holds each run to the outcomes probes.json wrote for its revision, which it tells from the registry class's sha256 on the driver's first line (any bytes but the two releases' are the mutant): an unpredicted outcome inside the claims' domain or the controls is a replay problem, outside it a reported difference. Its self-test tells the fix from six constructed registries: always-MVC (5.8.4's shape), always-Ant, reject-all, first-registration-only (the mutant's), reject-ambiguous-else-MVC (only the no-DispatcherServlet assertion fails it) and exact-class-equality (only the subclass probes outside the domain tell it).

Imported on 2026-11-14 from the archived registry (llm-dlc/loops/example-targets-inputs/spring-cve-targets.research-2026-11-04.json, as of 2026-11-04, rank 6, priority P1). Its capability notes are from verifier 4c279ba6 and stale; the blockers in target.json are predictions, with one more predicted from example 286's observed refusals (preservation's two closures, and the route's missing adapter entry).

Revisions checked against upstream on 2026-11-14, and again on 2026-11-16 for the setup: the release tags resolved to commits, each fix commit and its parent read from github.com, and the fix an ancestor of the fixed release and not of the vulnerable one.
Proof boundary (research): configuration selection or startup rejection is a local theorem. Authorization correctness requires composition with servlet mappings and actual request matching.

Feasibility (research): Medium. Strong configuration-selection example with new-API introduction. Needs classpath/reflection/servlet metadata models; preservation of every legacy configuration is not the correct fix contract because deliberate startup rejection is the mitigation. The plan's direction: the security claim on 5.8.5 first (the rejection comes before any matcher is made: the registry's initializer, the carriers, a LinkedHashMap's put, size and values() in order, ClassUtils.resolveClassName, Class.forName with the servlet classes' initializers, and Class.isAssignableFrom), then the two refutations, then preservation; stop after about four hours if the first step's models are not in place.

The proof loop, 2026-11-16, beside the route (proofs/prove.py, through the adapter entry). fixed-security is established at the frozen bound: job 20261116-225709-example-290-fixed-security-through-the-a, 6.9 s, 659 paths. What the path needed of the verifier, each now there with its evidence (lib/tests/claims.rs, claims.M and claims.Tables): a LinkedHashMap whose values are iterated in insertion order; an int's digits in a concatenation (the registrations' names); Class.forName(String) with initialization, Class.isAssignableFrom and the thread's context class loader; and, the new kind, three library initializers the checker does not run (Spring's ClassUtils; the servlet API's GenericServlet and HttpServlet), observed on a JVM on the revision's class path and their static state taken from there (--observed-initializer, lib/src/observed.rs). A result that used an observation says so: it is one run of the initializer on one JDK, taken to be what it leaves in every run, which is weaker than an initializer the checker ran. The registry's own initializer, the vulnerable code's, runs as written. The claims' expressions agree with the oracle on the 27 select probes (proofs/predicates.py). mutant-security is refuted at the frozen bound on servlets {1, 0} with no pattern, the witness run on a JVM: job 20261116-231724-example-290-mutant-security-through-the, 5.9 s, 708 paths. vulnerable-security has no verdict: 5.8.4 collects its matchers in ArrayLists, which the checker has no model of. A model written in the same session gave the expected witness and was taken out again, because the verifier's own conformance corpus records ArrayList as unmodelled and changing that is a step to make and review on its own. preservation is not attempted: it needs that model and the matchers' constructors. target.json's handoff has the details.

The proof loop, 2026-11-17, beside the route: all four proof tasks are decided at the frozen bound by proofs/prove.py at one commit, in one job (20261117-002240-example-290-the-four-proof-tasks-through, 38.9 s for the four after the build, peak 189 MiB). vulnerable-security is refuted: select(servlets=[0, 0], method=0, patterns={}) returns 0 on 5.8.4 and throws nothing, run on a JVM (4 paths; the search stops at its first witness, and the replay has 5.8.4 failing at all 12 ambiguous probes). preservation is established: outside the allowed change, that is with the DispatcherServlet the only servlet, the adapter compiled against each release returns the same count for every method and every array of patterns (573 paths, 7,907 variables), and a control with a wider region that must agree is refuted at a lone plain servlet, where the fix changes the selection by design. What was missing the day before, each now in the verifier with its evidence: a model of java.util.ArrayList that the checker runs only for a check that asks for it (prove --model; it is on request because new ArrayList(int) is the gap the contract library, the conformance corpus and other examples' recorded refusals are written about); Arrays.copyOf of an array of references; new ConcurrentHashMap() and new ConcurrentHashMap(int) as objects with no content; and, for the pair of releases, the previous release's questions by name answered on its own class path (Class.forName called by a copy of its code finds the copy, a copy's getName() is the class's own name) with each observed initializer observed in each release on that release's class path (lib/tests/claims.rs, lib/tests/pairing.rs). What the verdicts rest on beyond the bytecode: up to five library initializers per release observed on a JVM instead of run by the checker (ClassUtils, GenericServlet, HttpServlet, UrlPathHelper, AntPathMatcher), the hand-written ArrayList model, and the stated class-loader assumptions; each outcome lists the ones its paths used. These are answers beside the route: it has no adapter entry, so there are no route receipts for the four tasks.

2026-11-17, the user's review (decision prove-change-D005, VF-033): read 290's results at exactly their scope. Preservation is established for the count of matchers by type in the lone-DispatcherServlet configuration, not for the matchers themselves (pattern, HTTP method, servlet path) or what they match; a restated claim comparing what the matchers are is queued for a later run. fixed-security and preservation start from library initializers observed once on a JVM: two of them load resource bundles (default locale, class loader resources), so 'no input' is the outcome's assumption, not a checked fact, and those verdicts hold under it until the state they read is audited. The vulnerable and mutant refutations replay on a JVM and do not rest on it.

The acceptance check with the driver's record (2026-11-17, `python3 examples/tools/accept.py 290`). Job 20261117-133148-example-290-the-four-answers-beside-the reran the four tasks unchanged at the frozen bound, with the same observed initializers, through proofs/prove.py on examples/tools/beside_route.py, which writes evidence.json beside each outcome (the JARs of each class path with their hashes, the adapter's sources and classes, the claim file, the bound and the verifier's binary) and ends the run when the mutant's JAR is not the one the mutant replay ran. The same four verdicts, with the same path counts (preservation 573, vulnerable-security 4, fixed-security 659, mutant-security 708), in 45.9 s. Each task's besideRoute names that job, and accept.py accepts all four from it with no limit: every JAR the one target.json pins (the mutant's, but for its own JAR, its base's), the verifier's binary recorded (sha256 14673718…). The observed initializers' audit (VF-033) is separate: an acceptance says the answer is the one the evidence gives, and the outcome's restsOn still lists each observation.

Vacuity outside the allowed change (2026-11-17, the evidence stream's step 4). The preservation outcome of jobs 20261117-002240 and 20261117-133148 named the witness agree(servlets=[], method=4, patterns={null x8}), which lies inside the allowed change `!(servlets.length == 1 && servlets[0] == 0)`: on it `agree` returns true without calling either version, so that witness showed no comparison (the property check's probe asked only for an input of the assumption; see example 289's notes for the control). With the fix (lib/src/pairing.rs) a capped probe run of this task through proofs/prove.py is still verified, and non-vacuous with the witness agree(servlets=[0], method=4, patterns={null x8}), outside the change, as the outcome now says (`stated.vacuity.outside`). accept.py refuses the recorded preservation answer until a run of a checker with the fix answers it.

2026-11-17, the challenge stream (domain-advances, item 1): the accepted preservation result is the pair of versions' (lib/src/pairing.rs), which compares an exception by its category in harness::EXCEPTIONS, not its class, while the claim says 'throw the same exception'. Two unrelated RuntimeExceptions outside the list, or an IllegalArgumentException and a subclass of it, 'agree' there (countermodels in lib/tests/fixtures/pairing-countermodels, proved to agree though a JVM tells them apart). So the result says less than its claim on any input of the domain where both releases throw different classes of one category; whether there is such an input is not shown. Not affected by the pair's other holes: the run passes --before-classpath (no library static shared), its allowed change calls no code of either release, and the adapter sets no default locale. Open until the preservation stream's pairing compares exceptions by class and the task is rerun; the record is the challenge brief's Progress.

2026-11-17, the challenge stream (domain-advances, item 5, after the preservation stream's wokytpkz): the pair of versions now compares an exception by its class's name and the names of the classes above it up to Object, which answers the item 1 note above. What it does not compare is the rest of what a caller's handler can read of an exception: the interfaces its class implements, its message, and its own fields. lib/tests/fixtures/thrown-pair-countermodels has three pairs, each proved to agree with no stated assumption where a handler tells the versions apart on a JVM. Could a wrong implementation satisfy this claim? A release that throws the same class with another message, or with another interface or field, satisfies the claim as the pair reads it. In this example's pinned JARs, no class named *Exception or *Error differs between the releases in what it extends, what it implements, or its members (javap -p), so the interface and field cases cannot occur here. Whether a message differs on the domain was not checked. The claim's 'the same exception' is one class name and one chain of superclass names, and it should say so, or the pair should compare the message too (sent to the preservation stream).

The observed initializers, audited and bound (2026-11-17, the evidence stream's step 5; VF-033's audit half). fixed-security and preservation start five classes from the static state a JVM left (`--observed-initializer`): ClassUtils and AntPathMatcher of spring-core 5.3.28/29, UrlPathHelper of spring-web 5.3.28/29, GenericServlet and HttpServlet of jakarta.servlet-api 4.0.4. The audit (the challenge stream, from the pinned, hash-checked JARs with javap -c; lib/tests/fixtures/observed-countermodels/README.md): no <clinit> of the five writes a static of another class; GenericServlet and HttpServlet read the default locale, through ResourceBundle.getBundle, into lStrings, a field the observation does not hold (a read of it is refused by name); UrlPathHelper asks commons-logging for a Log, also not held. So the outside review's countermodels (an initializer that writes another class's static, one observed under a Turkish default locale, one that read a system property) do not reach 290's verdicts. The checker now binds an observation to what it was observed on (lib/src/observed.rs, `On`) and ends the run where it is not: the class file the JVM initialized must be the one the tool reads on the same class path in the same order; each class of the class path the initialization also initialized must be left as it is initialized alone in a JVM of its own (ClassUtils initializes ConcurrentReferenceHashMap with three nested classes and Assert; UrlPathHelper those, LogFactory and LogAdapter's classes; each is the same alone); a default locale of tr, az or lt is refused; the properties the class path's code read are stated with their values. A capped probe of fixed-security and preservation with that checker (same driver, same JARs) verified both again with the same path counts (659 and 573), each observation stated as read in en-US, reading no system property; lib/tests/observed_countermodels.rs `an_observed_initializer_is_bound_to_what_it_was_observed_on` holds the three countermodels refused or stated. The accepted outcomes predate the binding and do not state it; the preservation rerun that step 3 still owes (with zmvkptqz) will.

The restated preservation claim, prepared and not frozen (2026-11-17, the evidence stream; VF-033's option B, the user's choice). claims/lone-dispatcher-matchers-preserved.json (sha256 4185eea3…) compares what the matchers are, not how many of each type: on the same table, assumption, allowed change, observations and bound as lone-dispatcher-selection-preserved.json, both releases return matchers of the same exact classes, in the same order, with the same pattern, HTTP method and servlet path, for both overloads, or throw in the same category. Its entry is a new adapter class, replay/adapter/example290/adapter/MatcherDescriptionAdapter.java (describe: the same setup and call as select, then one line per matcher: its exact class, the length of its toString() and that text, which is the library's rendering of the pattern, the servlet path and the method); MatcherSelectionAdapter is left as it is, since the frozen claims and the recorded answers name it. On a JVM, outside any proof: describe on 168 probes of both releases agrees on all 28 with the DispatcherServlet alone and differs on 132 of the rest where the fix changes the selection by design. Stated in the claim, not assumed away: an MvcRequestMatcher renders a null pattern and the pattern "null" alike (seen on that JVM run), and an AntPathRequestMatcher's case sensitivity is not rendered. Where the checker stands, from two capped probes through proofs/prove.py in a scratch copy with the task pointed at the new claim: at bound 1 (a trial) it stops at its first gap, StringBuilder.append(Object) in MvcRequestMatcher.toString (the HTTP method appended as an object), unverifiable in 6 s (29 paths); at the frozen bound 8 the probe reached the 4 GiB cap after 133 s with no verdict, so the proof is a job. Freezing it is the user's: record the file's hash in a claims ledger (llm-dlc/decisions/*-claims.json), point the preservation task's claim at it and add the adapter source to preparation.adapters; proofs/prove.py then runs describe for that task by itself (ENTRIES), and examples/tools/accept.py keeps accepting the three security answers, whose job did not compile the new source (it is reported as listed since). The proof needs the checker to append an enum constant to a StringBuilder first (its toString, Enum's name), then one job at the frozen bound.

The binding, widened (2026-11-17, the evidence stream, inbox item I008 from the challenge stream's `ob` countermodels, lib/tests/fixtures/rule-countermodels): an observation is now also bound to its supertypes' state (a superclass or superinterface the initialization initialized must be left as it is alone, where before it was skipped), to a system property read by key through the map System.getProperties() gives (stated as any read), to a read of the properties as a whole and to code that reads the environment (System.getenv, ProcessBuilder.environment: both refused), and states the default time zone. A capped probe of fixed-security and preservation through proofs/prove.py with that checker verified both again with the same path counts (659 and 573): HttpServlet's initialization initializes its superclass GenericServlet, the same alone; none of the observed classes or the classes they initialize reads the environment or the properties as a whole; each observation states en-US and Etc/UTC and no system property read. The accepted outcomes predate the binding and do not state the time zone; the preservation rerun that step 3 still owes will.

The binding, widened again (2026-11-17, the evidence stream, inbox item I011 from the challenge stream's binding countermodels, lib/tests/fixtures/binding-countermodels): a class the initialization initialized besides is now compared with its state alone in full, a value the observation does not hold by the observer's description of it (an object's fields, a lambda's method and captured values, a JDK collection's elements, a float's bits), and one the observer does not describe is refused; and the observer reads the default locale, the time zone and the system properties again after the initialization, refusing one that changed. So bc.Boxed (a write into the Box another class holds), bc.Rehooked (a lambda of Hooks put in place of another) and bc.Relocaled (Locale.setDefault) are refused (lib/tests/observed_countermodels.rs). For 290: the nine classes ClassUtils's and UrlPathHelper's initializations initialize, and GenericServlet beside HttpServlet, hold two IdentityHashMaps of classes, a HashSet of interfaces, an empty ConcurrentReferenceHashMap, enum constants, a resource bundle and a float, each described and the same alone; no setting changed. A capped probe of fixed-security and preservation through proofs/prove.py with that checker verified both again with the same path counts (659 and 573). Not compared, and said in lib/src/observed.rs: the JDK's own state beyond those settings (spring-jcl's LogFactory may register a logger with the JDK's logging; 290's adapters name no logger), and what a ReferenceQueue holds.

Preservation accepted again (2026-11-18, the preservation stream, by the user's D036). The task record now names job 20261117-213024-examples-289-and-290-preservation-again, step 2, which reran preservation at the frozen bound 8 into verification/.work-290/closed-fields: verified, 573 paths, unwinding 64 complete, its witness agree(servlets=[0], method=4, patterns={null x8}) outside the allowed change, where the older jobs' witness servlets=[] lay inside it. `accept.py 290` accepts it with 13 checks and no recorded limit. The pair compares an exception by its class's name, the interfaces it implements and the names of the classes above it up to Object, gives each version its own copies of the array arguments, and checks the allowed change on inputs outside it (vacuity.outside); an exception's message, cause and own fields are not compared, as the challenge stream's item 5 note above says. The checker was at source commit 6d515865 (the observer's absolute log path, the reach resolving each field to its declaring class); JDK 25.0.5. The one-function rule's side conditions (I023, later) do not bear on this result: no call was taken as one function of both versions here, and a capped probe after them verified it again.

examples.title: spring-security@fe9e4549: BCrypt.hashpw with StandardCharsets.UTF_8 (positive scaffold)
examples.summary: Security's 2019 change of `BCrypt.hashpw(String,String)` from `password.getBytes("UTF-8")` with an AssertionError wrapper to `password.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)`. The positive of the password-bytes family: on fixed salts from upstream's tests and a frozen password domain (null, malformed surrogates and invalid salts included), both revisions should return the same hash or exception class. A partial scaffold: source-locked, claim frozen, oracle, driver, probes and mutant written; not yet built or run through the pipeline.
notes: A positive scaffold of llm-dlc/loops/example-targets.md (positive stream): an expected outcome for named claims on one upstream change, never a statement that the release is secure. Readiness and proof outcomes come from receipts, not from this file.
Source lock checked upstream on 2026-11-14 (sources.lock.json): fe9e4549's only parent is fb39d9c2.

No Central artifact has either side's exact BCrypt.java: before's is 5.2.0.M4's (repo.spring.io only); 5.2.0.RELEASE drops an unused import and a `final` on private encipher. The upstream build needs services.gradle.org and repo.spring.io, allowed by decision 1's extension (2026-11-14), and pins no SNAPSHOT; but its build plugin spring-build-conventions 0.0.23.RELEASE is on no anonymous repository (repo.spring.io answers 401, plugins.gradle.org redirects to Central, which has 404; HEAD requests, 2026-11-14), so the build is predicted to stop at its buildscript.

This pair has no length restriction of its own: CVE-2025-22228's 72-byte guard came in 2025. BCrypt's key schedule uses at most 72 password bytes on both revisions, which the 71, 72 and 73-byte probes observe without importing the later policy.

The packet (2026-11-14): claims/hashpw-preservation.json (a null password or one of at most 80 UTF-16 code units of any values; seven fixed salts in an assume expression; the returned String or the exception class; maxArrayLength 80, unwind 513, which completes every loop on this domain); replay/probes.json (45 probes; the salts and three known answers from upstream's BCryptTests, blob dc242a49 at both commits); controls/oracle.py (UTF-8 encoded independently, a result decided by the salt and the first 72 bytes of the cyclic key with its NUL terminator, distinct keys assumed to give distinct results; no cipher); replay/driver (arguments as UTF-16 code units in hex); controls/us-ascii.patch (the mutant, on after's BCrypt.java, sha256 a2b4e97f...).

The domain decisions: a null password is in, NullPointerException even with a null salt (the conversion comes first); malformed surrogates are in, encoded as '?' as String.getBytes specifies for both overloads; four invalid salts from upstream's tests are in, IllegalArgumentException. The exception is observed by class only: since JDK 14 a NullPointerException's message names the method called on null, getBytes(String) at before and getBytes(Charset) at after, so the messages differ by the patch itself. One quirk is in the expectations: under the '$2$05$' salt (no minor revision, so no NUL terminator) an empty password is an empty key, and both revisions throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

A hand replay on 2026-11-14, a note and not evidence, since no side is the commit's build output: each commit's BCrypt.java compiled alone by javac 1.8.0_512 -source 8 -target 8 (before.jar sha256 2dd39ba5..., after.jar c078d233...), Central's spring-security-crypto-5.2.0.RELEASE.jar (3d0017d9..., sha1 checked against Central), and the driver by javac 21.0.13 --release 21 (driver.jar 8e8dac4d...), run on Temurin 21.0.13 and 25.0.5. Before, after and the published class agree with the oracle and with each other on all 45 probes, byte-identically on both JDKs; the three upstream known answers hold. The mutant (mutant.jar c3c8688d..., and in a copy of the published JAR f565d289...) breaks the oracle's key rules nine times and differs from before on 17 probes, all with non-ASCII passwords, the one-character 'é' among them.

Bytecode, by javap on the hand-built classes: before and after differ only in hashpw(String,String), apart from constant-pool indices (which turn some ldc_w in <clinit> into ldc); the published 5.2.0.RELEASE class differs from after's only in encipher's ACC_FINAL. That is what a checked summary of the unchanged callee hashpw(byte[],String) would be bound to.

A static jvmcontract gaps scan (records/hashpw-gaps.json, a note, with a binary one lib/src commit old) refuses the changed conversion itself on both sides: String.getBytes(String), String.getBytes(Charset), and the read of StandardCharsets.UTF_8. In the callee it also refuses Arrays.copyOf(byte[],int), and finds Integer.parseInt and StringBuilder.charAt with no approximation. Unlike 305, the strict attempt is predicted to stop at the change, not around it. W1's planner (workflow commit wqsyopql, run from a temporary copy) plans both tasks with this claim file.

Mutation control as a revision (2026-11-14, example-targets Phase 5): controls/us-ascii.patch is declared in target.json as workflow W1's constructed revision `mutant` (base `after`, the patch's sha256 locked), the after of the `mutation` pair. It has two tasks of its own: `mutant-replay`, the concrete controls on that pair, where the base must hold and the mutant fail the oracle, and `mutant-preservation`, preservation's claim on the mutant, expected refuted. Its claim is bound to the mutant's artifact (runtime's identity `mutant:<base commit>+<patch sha256>`), never to a release's. It used to be only a `controls` entry on `after`, which no task prepared.

Could a wrong implementation satisfy the claim? (2026-11-17, the domain-advances challenge stream, item 6.) Yes, on the claim's own JDKs. controls/default-charset.patch (sha256 5a8b30a3…) on after's BCrypt.java converts with password.getBytes(): the platform's default charset, the dependence the commit removes. Since JDK 18 (JEP 400) that default is UTF-8 unless file.encoding says otherwise. So on Temurin 25.0.5 the mutant is after byte for byte: its driver lines equal after's on all 45 probes, and the oracle finds no problem. hashpw-preservation on fb39d9c2 against it is predicted to be decided as it is against after. Run with -Dfile.encoding=COMPAT under LANG=C (the native charset ASCII), it differs from after on 17 probes, the non-ASCII ones us-ascii.patch breaks too. The claim says 'on one and the same JDK' and fixes no default charset, so it cannot show that the conversion no longer depends on the platform. An assumption that names the default charset as other than UTF-8, or a pair run under COMPAT, would.

Companions and tags (2026-11-14, example-targets Phase 5): target.json's identity names 287, this family's CVE packet, as its companion, as 287 names this one; the example is tagged external-target, as every example with a sidecar is, and password-hashing, its family's domain tag.

Runner interface (2026-11-14, example-targets Phase 5 step 1, request 9): controls/oracle.py also defines driver_args(), the driver's whole argument vector (the same as `oracle.py argv`), and problems(lines), one revision's driver lines in, [(probe, problem)] out, where the independent statement disagrees; an exception is a replay that can't be judged, never a violation. runtime.run_controls passes driver_args() and keeps every line the driver prints, its preparation copies the probes file with the oracle, and workflow_ingest reads each revision with problems() against what its pair's kind expects (examples/tools/targets/runtime.py's docstring). Before this, the merged runner looked for a PROBES list and ingestion called check(lines), so the controls could not have run. The CLI (`argv`, `check`, the pair comparison) is unchanged.

Tags (the user, 2026-11-14): authentication was dropped. Its vocabulary entry means tokens and their validation (JWT timestamps, signatures, skew), and this change only alters how BCrypt.hashpw turns a password into bytes; password-hashing and text-encoding describe it. Example 300 keeps the tag for DaoAuthenticationProvider's login timing.
